Reading Comprehension: Factual Passages127 questions

Q1CUET 2026 · 11 May, Shift 1 · Q41NTA final key
Passage (summarised): Dibrugarh and Sambalpur (Q41–45)

Summary in our own words; the exam printed the full travel piece.

With the first chill of the season, India’s forests come back to life. In western Odisha, Dibrugarh Wildlife Sanctuary near Sambalpur, about to be declared India’s newest tiger reserve, is drawing attention “not just for its Wildlife” but also for the local people who have helped it flourish. It spreads over forested slopes by the Hirakud reservoir: birdsong at dawn, spotted deer and langurs, eagles overhead, and on Bot Island “thousands of bats hang like dark fruits”. Once an overlooked woodland, it is now a leading story of eco-tourism and “community-led conservation”.

Sambalpur lies at the edge of this wilderness, along the Mahanadi River, which “runs through it all”. Its past runs from the Chauhan dynasty to colonial times; its present hums with trade, textiles and temple bells.

Nearby, Hirakud Dam (built 1950, one of the world’s longest earthen dams) is called an engineering marvel that tames the Mahanadi. In Sambalpur’s lanes the clicking looms are where the famous Sambalpuri ikat is woven, each fabric made with precision and patience. At festivals people wear ikat saris and handwoven kurtas, and the city becomes a living gallery.

Dibrugarh Wildlife Sanctuary is attracting tourists because of its-
  1. Wildlife
  2. Mahanadi River
  3. Community-led Conservation
  4. Engineering Marvel
Concept to recall“not just for X, but for Y” – both are named; the stress falls on Y.
  1. It draws attention “not just for its Wildlife” but for the people who helped it thrive, i.e. community-led conservation.
  2. The Mahanadi belongs to Sambalpur; the engineering marvel is Hirakud Dam.

Answer: option (3) — Community-led Conservation

NoteNTA’s final key accepts both (1) Wildlife and (3) Community-led Conservation, since the passage names both reasons.

Passage (summarised): Dibrugarh and Sambalpur (Q41–45)

Which of the following river runs through the city of Sambalpur?
  1. Western river
  2. Hirakund river
  3. Woodland river
  4. Mahanadi river
Concept to recallDirect fact: Sambalpur lies along the Mahanadi, which “runs through it all”.
  1. The Mahanadi is the only river named.
  2. “Western” describes Odisha; Hirakud is a dam/reservoir; “woodland” is the forest.

Answer: option (4) — Mahanadi river

Passage (summarised): Dibrugarh and Sambalpur (Q41–45)

Summary in our own words; the exam printed the full travel piece.

Once an overlooked woodland, it is now a leading story of eco-tourism and “community-led conservation”.

The main profession of the people in sambalpur is-
  1. Animal Training
  2. Wild life awakening
  3. Textile and weaving
  4. Engineering the dam
Concept to recallInference from repeated detail: textiles, looms, threads, ikat, handwoven garments.
  1. Sambalpur “hums with trade, textiles”; looms click in its lanes ⇒ textile and weaving.
  2. Animals and the “awakening” belong to the sanctuary; the dam is a structure, not a trade.

Q4CUET 2026 · 6 Jun, Shift 1 · Q41NTA final key
Passage (summarised): Declining Number of Elephants (Q41–45)

Summary in our own words; the exam printed the full article.

India’s elephants are in trouble. A Wildlife Institute of India estimate puts the 2025 count at 22,446, 17% below the 2017 count of 27,312. In 2024 the Centre had told the Lok Sabha that India’s “pachyderm population” was 29,964. The surveys use different methods and are not strictly comparable, and the DNA model may have under-counted – but there is still ample reason for concern.

The SAIFE report makes three points. (1) In the Western Ghats the once-continuous population is splintering because of changing land use – plantations, invasive plants, farmland fencing, encroachment and development projects – which affects elephant “survival and migration”. (2) In East Central India, mining and infrastructure projects have fragmented and degraded habitats, so long-ranging elephants enter human dwellings and human–wildlife conflict rises. (3) The North East, with the second-largest population, has lost habitat to resource exploitation since colonial times, with rising conflict. Conflicts and rail accidents in Kerala, West Bengal and Assam bear this out. Project Elephant (1992) “needs a renewed push”.

'Project Elephant' needs a renewed push because:
  1. wildlife surveys are not conclusive.
  2. farmland fencing has proved to be a boon.
  3. human-wildlife conflict is on the rise.
  4. the North East has the second largest elephant population.
Concept to recallFind the conclusion and what leads to it: habitat loss ⇒ elephants enter villages ⇒ rising conflict and accidents.
  1. All three inferences end in habitat loss and rising human–elephant conflict, confirmed by reports from Kerala, West Bengal and Assam.
  2. That is why Project Elephant needs a push.
  3. Inconclusive surveys are mentioned but dismissed; fencing is a harm, not a boon; the North East figure is a fact, not the reason.

Answer: option (3) — human-wildlife conflict is on the rise.

Q5CUET 2026 · 6 Jun, Shift 1 · Q42NTA final key
Passage (summarised): Declining Number of Elephants (Q41–45)

Summary in our own words; the exam printed the full article.

India’s elephants are in trouble. A Wildlife Institute of India estimate puts the 2025 count at 22,446, 17% below the 2017 count of 27,312. In 2024 the Centre had told the Lok Sabha that India’s “pachyderm population” was 29,964. The surveys use different methods and are not strictly comparable, and the DNA model may have under-counted – but there is still ample reason for concern.

The SAIFE report makes three points. (1) In the Western Ghats the once-continuous population is splintering because of changing land use – plantations, invasive plants, farmland fencing, encroachment and development projects – which affects elephant “survival and migration”. (2) In East Central India, mining and infrastructure projects have fragmented and degraded habitats, so long-ranging elephants enter human dwellings and human–wildlife conflict rises. (3) The North East, with the second-largest population, has lost habitat to resource exploitation since colonial times, with rising conflict. Conflicts and rail accidents in Kerala, West Bengal and Assam bear this out. Project Elephant (1992) “needs a renewed push”.

The changing land use in the Western Ghats is responsible for the---------------- of the elephant population.
  1. augmentation
  2. deterioration
  3. sickness
  4. migration
Concept to recallRead the exact sentence: land-use changes “impact elephant survival and migration”.
  1. NTA’s key: migration – the word the passage itself pairs with land-use change.
  2. Augmentation (increase) is the opposite; sickness is not mentioned.

Answer: option (4) — migration

TrapDeterioration appears in the passage, but in the paragraph on East Central India.
Note“Deterioration” (option 2) is arguably a better fit, since the population is “splintering” and the passage uses “deterioration” for the habitats of East Central India. NTA’s final key gives only option 4, and it is kept. The question rewards the word lifted from the line on the Western Ghats.

__________ have compelled the elephant population to invade human dwellings.
  1. Infrastructure projects
  2. Habitats in Central India
  3. Contiguous elephant population
  4. Health of the elephants
Concept to recallCause-and-effect: mining and infrastructure projects fragmented habitats ⇒ elephants ventured into human dwellings.
  1. Second inference: mining and infrastructure projects degrade habitats, prompting elephants into villages.
  2. The habitats are where it happens, not the cause; the other two are unrelated.

Answer: option (1) — Infrastructure projects

Q7CUET 2025 · 13 May, Shift 1 · Q10NTA final key
Passage (summarised): hidden hunger (Q9–12)

Summary in our own words; the exam printed the full extract.

Source named in the passage: the State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World report (2024). It found 733 million people facing malnutrition in 2023, 152 million more than in 2019.

The rise is tied to food prices: by a 2022 World Bank estimate, every 1% increase in world food prices could drive 10 million more people into extreme poverty. Rising costs and inequality have worsened “hidden hunger”, affecting at least 2.8 billion people in 2022.

Hidden hunger is a lack of micronutrients such as zinc, iodine and iron. It is “hidden” because people may look healthy while suffering serious harm; clinical signs appear only in extreme cases. Hunger, once linked only to too few calories, now includes micronutrient inadequacy.

The report says the link between food insecurity and a poor diet is complex, shaped by “food environments, consumer behaviour, and the affordability of nutritious foods”. Sometimes insecurity means eating less of everything and relying on staples; sometimes it means less nutritious food and more cheap energy-dense food high in fats, sugar and salt. So it can cause undernutrition and also overweight and obesity.

Which factor complicates the relationship between food insecurity and diet quality?
  1. The absence of global food production data.
  2. The overreliance on scientific studies rather than real-world evidence.
  3. Variations in food environments, consumer behaviour, and affordability
  4. The assumption that food insecurity always results in undernutrition.
Concept to recallLocate the key words: “the relationship is complex, shaped by factors like …”.
  1. Paragraph 4 names the factors: food environments, consumer behaviour, affordability of nutritious food.
  2. Options 1 and 2 are not in the passage.
  3. Option 4 is a belief the passage corrects, not a factor shaping the relationship.

Answer: option (3) — Variations in food environments, consumer behaviour, and affordability

TrapOption 4 sounds like the passage’s conclusion but answers a different question.
Q8CUET 2025 · 13 May, Shift 1 · Q11NTA final key
Passage (summarised): hidden hunger (Q9–12)

Summary in our own words; the exam printed the full extract.

Source named in the passage: the State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World report (2024). It found 733 million people facing malnutrition in 2023, 152 million more than in 2019.

The rise is tied to food prices: by a 2022 World Bank estimate, every 1% increase in world food prices could drive 10 million more people into extreme poverty. Rising costs and inequality have worsened “hidden hunger”, affecting at least 2.8 billion people in 2022.

Hidden hunger is a lack of micronutrients such as zinc, iodine and iron. It is “hidden” because people may look healthy while suffering serious harm; clinical signs appear only in extreme cases. Hunger, once linked only to too few calories, now includes micronutrient inadequacy.

The report says the link between food insecurity and a poor diet is complex, shaped by “food environments, consumer behaviour, and the affordability of nutritious foods”. Sometimes insecurity means eating less of everything and relying on staples; sometimes it means less nutritious food and more cheap energy-dense food high in fats, sugar and salt. So it can cause undernutrition and also overweight and obesity.

How can food insecurity paradoxically contribute to obesity?
  1. by causing people to eat excessive amounts of protein.
  2. by encouraging over consumption of cheap, unhealthy energy-dense foods.
  3. by limiting access to all food types, reducing overall consumption.
  4. by increasing the availability of nutrient-rich food in low-income areas.
Concept to recallLast paragraph: insecurity can mean more energy-dense foods high in fats, sugar and salt ⇒ overweight.
  1. The paradox: too little good food yet weight gain.
  2. Cause given: “increased consumption of energy-dense foods high in unhealthy fats, sugars, and salt”.
  3. Option 3 leads to undernutrition, not obesity; options 1 and 4 are not stated.

Answer: option (2) — by encouraging over consumption of cheap, unhealthy energy-dense foods.

TrapOption 3 is in the passage but is the other case (undernutrition).

What consequence does the World Bank estimate of a 1% rise in global food prices?
  1. A decline in global malnutrition rates.
  2. A reduction in food insecurity through economic growth.
  3. An increase of 10 million people towards extreme poverty.
  4. No significant impact on food security.
Concept to recallA direct fact question: find the sentence with “World Bank”.
  1. The passage: a 1% rise in global food prices could push 10 million people into extreme poverty.
  2. The other three say the opposite or nothing the passage states.

Answer: option (3) — An increase of 10 million people towards extreme poverty.

Q10CUET 2025 · 13 May, Shift 1 · Q9NTA final key
Passage (summarised): hidden hunger (Q9–12)

Summary in our own words; the exam printed the full extract.

Source named in the passage: the State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World report (2024). It found 733 million people facing malnutrition in 2023, 152 million more than in 2019.

The rise is tied to food prices: by a 2022 World Bank estimate, every 1% increase in world food prices could drive 10 million more people into extreme poverty. Rising costs and inequality have worsened “hidden hunger”, affecting at least 2.8 billion people in 2022.

Hidden hunger is a lack of micronutrients such as zinc, iodine and iron. It is “hidden” because people may look healthy while suffering serious harm; clinical signs appear only in extreme cases. Hunger, once linked only to too few calories, now includes micronutrient inadequacy.

The report says the link between food insecurity and a poor diet is complex, shaped by “food environments, consumer behaviour, and the affordability of nutritious foods”. Sometimes insecurity means eating less of everything and relying on staples; sometimes it means less nutritious food and more cheap energy-dense food high in fats, sugar and salt. So it can cause undernutrition and also overweight and obesity.

What is the primary distinction between "hidden hunger" and traditional caloric deficiency?
  1. Hidden hunger refers to a lack of protein, whereas caloric deficiency refers to a lack of fats.
  2. Hidden hunger is caused by excessive food intake, whereas caloric deficiency is caused by food scarcity.
  3. Hidden hunger involves not so obvious micronutrient deficiencies, while caloric deficiency has visible symptoms.
  4. Hidden hunger is a short-term condition, whereas caloric deficiency affects only long-term health.
Concept to recallHidden hunger = lack of micronutrients (zinc, iodine, iron) with no obvious signs.
  1. Paragraph 3: a deficiency of micronutrients; “hidden” because people may appear healthy.
  2. Traditional hunger = lack of calories, which shows.
  3. Protein/fat, overeating, short-term/long-term – none is in the passage.

Answer: option (3) — Hidden hunger involves not so obvious micronutrient deficiencies, while caloric deficiency has visible symptoms.

TrapOption 2 twists the last paragraph (energy-dense food) into “excessive intake” as a cause.
Q11CUET 2024 · 15 May (pen & paper) · Code A · Q23NTA final key
Passage (summarised): do we have free will? (Q23–28)

An opinion essay; the paper names no source.

The writer defines free will as deciding and acting with no influence from the past or the environment, and says we clearly lack it: our minds are conditioned. Memories, impressions and experiences shape present choices — our “karmic imprint”, i.e. the product of our genetic code, upbringing and environment, our “backstory”.

The only way to experience free will would be to shed this conditioning by letting go of ego, attachments and fixed beliefs. That is the strict definition. In the everyday sense (choosing a spouse, a profession, a reaction), our choices are still significantly restricted by our predispositions. Even our ability to change ourselves depends partly on emotional and mental wiring, which is why some people succeed more than others.

To expand one’s agency, the writer recommends sustained inner work, deeper self-awareness and re-examining conditioned beliefs — while wondering whether even the urge to do so is itself conditioned.

The author argues that humans don’t have “free will” because ____________________.
Fill in the blank with the correct option to complete the sentence.
  1. our decisions are shaped by past events and environmental influences.
  2. we are born with pre-determined choices that we are forced to make.
  3. we are always dictated by our mind to make irrational choices.
  4. human beings are born slaves of social constructs and expectations.
Concept to recallReading comprehension: answer from what the passage says, not from general knowledge; reject options that over-state (always, only, completely) or reverse the text.
  1. The author says our choices are never separate from our past: memories, impressions and experiences shape present thought and action.
  2. (2), (3), (4) add ideas the author never states (forced choices, irrationality, social slavery).

Answer: option (1) — our decisions are shaped by past events and environmental influences.

“Karmic imprint” referred to in the passage implies ___________________________.
Fill in the blank with the correct option to complete the sentence.
  1. the ability to bring about change in oneself.
  2. our genetic code, upbringing and environment.
  3. the truth of our being, our individuality.
  4. the wrong doings and vices of our past lives.
Concept to recallReading comprehension: answer from what the passage says, not from general knowledge; reject options that over-state (always, only, completely) or reverse the text.
  1. The passage equates the karmic imprint with the result of our genetic code, upbringing and environment.
  2. Option (4) is the popular religious sense of karma, not the passage’s definition.

Answer: option (2) — our genetic code, upbringing and environment.

TrapDo not import the everyday meaning of a term when the passage defines it.

“Free will” can be experienced if ___________________________.
Fill in the blank with the correct option to complete the sentence.
  1. we embrace our past experiences and conditioning.
  2. we make choices without considering the consequences.
  3. we let go of our ego, attachments and fixed beliefs.
  4. we accumulate more and more karmic imprints.
Concept to recallReading comprehension: answer from what the passage says, not from general knowledge; reject options that over-state (always, only, completely) or reverse the text.
  1. Free will is possible only by purifying the mind, i.e. letting go of ego, attachments and fixed beliefs.
  2. (1) and (4) are the opposite of getting rid of conditioning; (2) is not in the passage.

Answer: option (3) — we let go of our ego, attachments and fixed beliefs.

To expand one’s agency, the writer recommends sustained inner work, deeper self-awareness and re-examining conditioned beliefs — while wondering whether even the urge to do so is itself conditioned.

The author proves that the idea of “free will” is a myth by suggesting that ______________________.
Fill in the blank with the correct option to complete the sentence.
  1. our ability to make a choice is restricted by our predispositions.
  2. we are unable to bring a change in ourselves.
  3. our choices are solely guided by the current environment.
  4. our choices are completely independent of past events and our genetic code.
Concept to recallReading comprehension: answer from what the passage says, not from general knowledge; reject options that over-state (always, only, completely) or reverse the text.
  1. Even everyday choices, the author says, are “significantly restricted” by our predispositions.
  2. (2) over-states: change depends partly on wiring, and some people succeed. (3) solely and (4) completely independent contradict the passage.

Answer: option (1) — our ability to make a choice is restricted by our predispositions.

Q15CUET 2024 · 15 May (pen & paper) · Code A · Q27NTA final key
Passage (summarised): do we have free will? (Q23–28)

An opinion essay; the paper names no source.

The writer defines free will as deciding and acting with no influence from the past or the environment, and says we clearly lack it: our minds are conditioned. Memories, impressions and experiences shape present choices — our “karmic imprint”, i.e. the product of our genetic code, upbringing and environment, our “backstory”.

The only way to experience free will would be to shed this conditioning by letting go of ego, attachments and fixed beliefs. That is the strict definition. In the everyday sense (choosing a spouse, a profession, a reaction), our choices are still significantly restricted by our predispositions. Even our ability to change ourselves depends partly on emotional and mental wiring, which is why some people succeed more than others.

To expand one’s agency, the writer recommends sustained inner work, deeper self-awareness and re-examining conditioned beliefs — while wondering whether even the urge to do so is itself conditioned.

What does the author propose as a means to expand the scope of one’s agency ?
Choose the correct option.
  1. Making choices frequently and impulsively.
  2. Engaging in sustained inner work and self-awareness.
  3. Holding on to fixed beliefs and stringent mindsets.
  4. Ignoring one’s past experiences and dispositions.
Concept to recallReading comprehension: answer from what the passage says, not from general knowledge; reject options that over-state (always, only, completely) or reverse the text.
  1. To expand one’s agency the author recommends sustained inner work and deeper self-awareness.
  2. The author asks us to examine and reform beliefs, not hold on to them (3) or ignore the past (4).

Answer: option (2) — Engaging in sustained inner work and self-awareness.

Q17CUET 2024 · 15 May (pen & paper) · Code A · Q29NTA final key
Passage (summarised): a short history of hot chocolate (Q29–34)

A magazine-style feature; it cites Bertram Gordon’s book Chocolate: History, Culture and Heritage.

The Olmec people of Central America first drank chocolate around 1500 BCE; the Aztec word xocolatl (enjoyed by Emperor Montezuma) gave English “chocolate”. The Aztecs did not serve it hot, and with no sugar yet they flavoured it with peppers and spices; it seemed more palatable because they believed chocolate was a divine gift with healing properties.

After the Spanish reached the Americas in the 1500s, chocolate travelled to Europe, where the wealthy added sugar and drank it warm; because sugar was still a luxury it became “the beverage of the aristocracy”. Soon it “caught on with the masses”: chocolate houses, part café and part casino, spread in 17th-century Europe, but mostly died off by the end of the 18th century, partly because chocolate cost much more than coffee or tea.

Today Italians serve it thick like pudding, Colombians with a dollop of soft cheese, Mexicans with vanilla, chilli and cinnamon, and Filipinos with mango chunks.

Cocoa was first introduced by the
  1. American people.
  2. Olmec people.
  3. Aztec people.
  4. Spanish people.
Concept to recallReading comprehension: answer from what the passage says, not from general knowledge; reject options that over-state (always, only, completely) or reverse the text.
  1. The Olmec people were the first to drink chocolate, around 1500 BCE.
  2. The Aztecs came later (Montezuma); the Spanish carried it to Europe in the 1500s.

Answer: option (2) — Olmec people.

Q22CUET 2024 · 15 May (pen & paper) · Code A · Q35NTA final key
Passage (summarised): the genetics of coffee (Q35–40)

A science news report quoting geneticist Juan Medrano (UC Davis Coffee Center).

About 10 million tonnes of coffee were sold in 2022–23. It comes from two species: Coffea Canephora (Robusta) and Coffea Arabica (Arabica). Beans are blended, but single-species beans are also roasted and sold; Arabica is about 56% of all coffee sold.

Most genetic variation comes from hybridising with other species, but this is rare for Arabica because it is polyploid — more than two copies of each chromosome — whereas Canephora has two. So Arabica’s main source of variation is mutation at a steady rate. Arabica is also young: it arose as a hybrid of Robusta and Coffea Eugenioides (little cultivated) within the past 50,000 years, so its variation consists only of mutations since then.

Even so, Arabica plants vary noticeably in bean flavour and disease resistance. Medrano notes that variability is low “at the DNA level” but present at the structural and chromosomal levels and in deletions and insertions.

Which of the following varieties of coffee is the most sold in the world ?
  1. Coffea Canephora
  2. Coffea Arabica
  3. Coffea Eugenioides
  4. A blend of Coffea Canephora and Coffea Arabica
Concept to recallReading comprehension: answer from what the passage says, not from general knowledge; reject options that over-state (always, only, completely) or reverse the text.
  1. “Overall, Arabica beans represent around 56% of all coffee sold” — more than half.
  2. Blends exist (4) but no share is given; Eugenioides is “not widely cultivated”.

Answer: option (2) — Coffea Arabica

Q28CUET 2024 · 29 May (Delhi re-scheduled) · Code A · Q1NTA final key
Passage (summarised): zinc against coughs and colds (Q1–6)

A health feature; the paper names no source.

Everyone knows vitamin C helps with colds, but few know the “secret solution” — zinc. Zinc reduces the severity and length of respiratory infections, soothes sore throats through its anti-inflammatory action, plays a “pivotal role” in immunity, wound healing and general health, stops viruses multiplying and boosts the immune system.

Zinc is found in a variety of plant and animal foods; eat them in moderation and with variety — lean meat, poultry, seafood, dairy, nuts, seeds — and combine them with vitamin C sources for stronger immunity.

Phytates in unprocessed whole grains block zinc absorption, so vegetarians should soak grains for 5–6 hours; fermented foods such as buttermilk and yogurt improve absorption. Too much supplemental zinc hinders absorption of other minerals, so consult a professional. Finally: “Stay hydrated”, cook in ways that preserve zinc, and watch for phytates.

According to the passage, combining zinc-rich foods with vitamin C will result in
  1. reduced immunity.
  2. increased immunity.
  3. food allergy.
  4. a sore throat.
Concept to recallReading comprehension: answer from what the passage says, not from general knowledge; reject options that over-state (always, only, completely) or reverse the text.
  1. The passage advises combining them “for enhanced immune support”.
  2. (1) is the reverse; allergy and sore throat are never linked to the combination.

Answer: option (2) — increased immunity.

Q29CUET 2024 · 29 May (Delhi re-scheduled) · Code A · Q10NTA final key
Passage (summarised): why pollinators matter (Q7–12)

The paper prints the heading “The Human Genome Project” over this passage — a misprint: the passage is about pollinators.

Pollinators — bees, butterflies, birds, bats — are vital to ecosystems, health and food security. By transferring pollen between flowers they let plants make seeds and fruit. This “mutualistic relationship” supports world food supply: about 75% of leading food crops depend on animal pollination. Pollinators also sustain the diversity of flowering plants, which provide habitat and food for other organisms.

They face serious threats. Habitat loss from urbanization, agriculture and deforestation reduces “nesting sites” and flowers. Pesticides (especially insecticides) and climate change further endanger them, by poisoning them and by disrupting their behaviour and reproduction.

Protection needs concerted action: restoring habitats, pollinator-friendly farming, less pesticide and more public awareness — securing ecosystems, biodiversity and food for the future.

Climate change endangers pollinator population by_________________.
  1. enabling the production of seeds and fruits
  2. disrupting their behaviour and reproductive patterns
  3. contributing to the abundance of flowering plants
  4. poisoning them
Concept to recallReading comprehension: answer from what the passage says, not from general knowledge; reject options that over-state (always, only, completely) or reverse the text.
  1. Pesticides and climate change are said to endanger pollinators by poisoning them and by disrupting their behaviour and reproduction. Disruption fits climate change; poisoning fits pesticides.
  2. Because the sentence joins both causes and both effects, NTA accepted (4) as well.
  3. (1) and (3) are benefits, not dangers.

Answer: option (2) — disrupting their behaviour and reproductive patterns

NoteNTA’s final key accepts both option (2) and option (4); either earned the marks.

Q31CUET 2024 · 29 May (Delhi re-scheduled) · Code A · Q13NTA final key
Passage (summarised): leaders and the ego (Q13–18)

A management column; the paper names no source.

The dictionary defines ego as your idea or opinion of yourself, especially your sense of self-importance and ability. In itself this is harmless; knowing oneself is an advantage, a reality check vital to contentment and to relationships. Everyone has an ego — only a liar or an ignorant person would deny it.

The trouble begins when the self “start[s] ballooning” into egotism: it derails leaders and creates havoc for colleagues. Senior leaders are most at risk because, out of deference or fear, juniors tell them what they like to hear.

Leaders must manage this “powerful asset” well, which can multiply their impact. Where they lack competence they should seek regular, genuine feedback (not a ceremonial annual exercise); for situations that bring out their worst — temper, impatience, feeling clever at others’ expense — they should study their own interactions from outside and set goals to reduce such lapses, often with professional help.

According to the passage, ego means
  1. our view of the cognitive world.
  2. an inflated view of ourselves.
  3. our view of others.
  4. a balanced view of oneself.
Concept to recallReading comprehension: answer from what the passage says, not from general knowledge; reject options that over-state (always, only, completely) or reverse the text.
  1. The passage defines ego as one’s idea of oneself and calls it harmless in itself; it only becomes a problem when it balloons. So the neutral sense is a (balanced) view of oneself.
  2. Since the quoted definition stresses self-importance, NTA also accepted (2).
  3. (1) and (3) are not about the self.

Answer: option (4) — a balanced view of oneself.

NoteNTA’s final key accepts both option (2) and option (4); either earned the marks.
Q32CUET 2024 · 29 May (Delhi re-scheduled) · Code A · Q14NTA final key
Passage (summarised): leaders and the ego (Q13–18)

A management column; the paper names no source.

The dictionary defines ego as your idea or opinion of yourself, especially your sense of self-importance and ability. In itself this is harmless; knowing oneself is an advantage, a reality check vital to contentment and to relationships. Everyone has an ego — only a liar or an ignorant person would deny it.

The trouble begins when the self “start[s] ballooning” into egotism: it derails leaders and creates havoc for colleagues. Senior leaders are most at risk because, out of deference or fear, juniors tell them what they like to hear.

Leaders must manage this “powerful asset” well, which can multiply their impact. Where they lack competence they should seek regular, genuine feedback (not a ceremonial annual exercise); for situations that bring out their worst — temper, impatience, feeling clever at others’ expense — they should study their own interactions from outside and set goals to reduce such lapses, often with professional help.

‘Knowing oneself’ is important because
  1. it leads to stress.
  2. it is a liability.
  3. it is an asset.
  4. it leads one to the black hole area.
Concept to recallReading comprehension: answer from what the passage says, not from general knowledge; reject options that over-state (always, only, completely) or reverse the text.
  1. Knowing oneself is called “always an advantage”, and ego is a “powerful asset”.
  2. (1), (2), (4) describe an inflated ego, not self-knowledge.

Answer: option (3) — it is an asset.

Q36CUET 2024 · 29 May (Delhi re-scheduled) · Code A · Q3NTA final key
Passage (summarised): zinc against coughs and colds (Q1–6)

A health feature; the paper names no source.

Everyone knows vitamin C helps with colds, but few know the “secret solution” — zinc. Zinc reduces the severity and length of respiratory infections, soothes sore throats through its anti-inflammatory action, plays a “pivotal role” in immunity, wound healing and general health, stops viruses multiplying and boosts the immune system.

Zinc is found in a variety of plant and animal foods; eat them in moderation and with variety — lean meat, poultry, seafood, dairy, nuts, seeds — and combine them with vitamin C sources for stronger immunity.

Phytates in unprocessed whole grains block zinc absorption, so vegetarians should soak grains for 5–6 hours; fermented foods such as buttermilk and yogurt improve absorption. Too much supplemental zinc hinders absorption of other minerals, so consult a professional. Finally: “Stay hydrated”, cook in ways that preserve zinc, and watch for phytates.

In the passage, which of the following is not a benefit connected to consuming zinc ?
  1. Strengthens immune system
  2. Anti-viral properties
  3. Anti-inflammatory agent
  4. Supports hair growth
Concept to recallReading comprehension: answer from what the passage says, not from general knowledge; reject options that over-state (always, only, completely) or reverse the text.
  1. Immunity, stopping viruses and anti-inflammatory action are all named.
  2. Hair growth is never mentioned.

Answer: option (4) — Supports hair growth

Q39CUET 2024 · 29 May (Delhi re-scheduled) · Code A · Q7NTA final key
Passage (summarised): why pollinators matter (Q7–12)

The paper prints the heading “The Human Genome Project” over this passage — a misprint: the passage is about pollinators.

Pollinators — bees, butterflies, birds, bats — are vital to ecosystems, health and food security. By transferring pollen between flowers they let plants make seeds and fruit. This “mutualistic relationship” supports world food supply: about 75% of leading food crops depend on animal pollination. Pollinators also sustain the diversity of flowering plants, which provide habitat and food for other organisms.

They face serious threats. Habitat loss from urbanization, agriculture and deforestation reduces “nesting sites” and flowers. Pesticides (especially insecticides) and climate change further endanger them, by poisoning them and by disrupting their behaviour and reproduction.

Protection needs concerted action: restoring habitats, pollinator-friendly farming, less pesticide and more public awareness — securing ecosystems, biodiversity and food for the future.

Choose the correct option to fill in the blank.
Pollinators help in plant reproduction by________________.
  1. transferring pollen between flowers
  2. securing human food
  3. fighting climate change
  4. providing food resources to various organisms
Concept to recallReading comprehension: answer from what the passage says, not from general knowledge; reject options that over-state (always, only, completely) or reverse the text.
  1. Plant reproduction happens through the transfer of pollen between flowers.
  2. Food security (2) and resources for other organisms (4) are consequences, not the mechanism; (3) is not claimed.

Answer: option (1) — transferring pollen between flowers

Q42CUET 2024 · 19 Jul re-test · Shift 1 · Q10NTA final key
Passage (summarised): Five a Day (Q7–12)

Titled “Five a Day” in the paper; a nutrition news report.

A new study supports the old guideline that five daily servings of varied fruits and vegetables are linked to longer life. People who ate two fruits and three vegetables a day had, compared with those eating two servings, a 12% lower risk of death from heart disease, 10% from cancer and 35% from respiratory disease.

A serving is 125 mL of fruit or vegetables or 250 mL of salad greens. Both give vitamins, minerals and fibre, but vegetables are lower in calories and sugar, so guidelines recommend eating more of them. The work combined two large American studies (over 1,00,000 people, followed up to 30 years) with 24 other studies into a meta-analysis of 1.8 million participants.

Variety matters, since different produce supplies different nutrients and antioxidants. Most produce was linked to lower mortality, but fruit juices and starchy vegetables (peas, corn, potatoes) were not — perhaps because of their higher glycaemic load. Fresh, frozen or canned produce all count; freezing and canning preserve nutrients and can make these foods “even more nutrient-dense” than fresh ones, helping people for whom fresh produce is costly or hard to get.

On the basis of your reading of the passage, choose the statement that is INCORRECT.
  1. We must consume a variety of fruits and vegetables as they are high in nutritive value.
  2. Peas, corn and potatoes are associated with lower mortality rate.
  3. Fruit juices have high glycaemic index and are not associated with lower risk of death.
  4. Consuming fruit juices and starchy vegetables can heighten the risk of chronic diseases.
Concept to recallReading comprehension: answer from what the passage says, not from general knowledge; reject options that over-state (always, only, completely) or reverse the text.
  1. Peas, corn and potatoes were the exceptions — not associated with lower risk. So (2) is incorrect.
  2. (1) and (3) follow from the passage; (4) is a fair reading of “not associated with reduced risk”.

Answer: option (2) — Peas, corn and potatoes are associated with lower mortality rate.

Q45CUET 2024 · 19 Jul re-test · Shift 1 · Q13NTA final key
Passage (summarised): light colour and the body clock (Q13–18)

A science news report on a study published in Nature Human Behaviour.

Researchers from Basel University and the Technical University of Munich challenge earlier beliefs about how the colour of light affects the internal clock and sleep-wake rhythm. Unlike an earlier study on mice, theirs suggests colour matters less than thought.

In the eye, photoreceptors turn light into electrical impulses passed via ganglion cells to the visual cortex. Specialised ganglion cells, sensitive to short-wavelength (blue, about 490 nm) light, tell the internal clock that it is daytime.

Sixteen volunteers were exposed for an hour in the late evening to bluish or yellowish light, with white light as a control. The stimuli were designed to activate the colour-sensitive cones selectively while stimulating the light-sensitive ganglion cells equally, so the effect of cone stimulation and light colour could be checked directly.

Contrary to the mouse findings — that yellowish light acted more strongly than bluish — colour did not significantly affect the clock. Light intensity and exposure time remain crucial, but colour may matter less than believed.

What does the recent study by researchers from the University of Basel and the Technical University of Munich challenge?
  1. sleep-wake rhythms in mice
  2. the impact of light colour on the internal clock
  3. vision complexity in humans
  4. the effect of sleep-wake cycle
Concept to recallReading comprehension: answer from what the passage says, not from general knowledge; reject options that over-state (always, only, completely) or reverse the text.
  1. It challenges prior beliefs about the influence of light colour on the internal clock.
  2. Mice (1) were the subject of the earlier study; (3) and (4) are background.

Answer: option (2) — the impact of light colour on the internal clock

NoteKey matched by Question ID 4641991517.

  1. Colour of light is the sole determinant of sleep and circadian rhythms.
  2. Light intensity plays a crucial role in sleep and circadian rhythms.
  3. Light intensity and exposure duration are the secondary factor.
  4. Light colour may not play as significant a role as previously believed.
Concept to recallReading comprehension: answer from what the passage says, not from general knowledge; reject options that over-state (always, only, completely) or reverse the text.
  1. The headline implication is that colour may matter less than believed.
  2. Intensity (2) is mentioned only as already-known background; (3) reverses the passage (they remain crucial); (1) is the opposite.

Answer: option (4) — Light colour may not play as significant a role as previously believed.

Q50CUET 2024 · 19 Jul re-test · Shift 1 · Q7NTA final key
Passage (summarised): Five a Day (Q7–12)

Titled “Five a Day” in the paper; a nutrition news report.

A new study supports the old guideline that five daily servings of varied fruits and vegetables are linked to longer life. People who ate two fruits and three vegetables a day had, compared with those eating two servings, a 12% lower risk of death from heart disease, 10% from cancer and 35% from respiratory disease.

A serving is 125 mL of fruit or vegetables or 250 mL of salad greens. Both give vitamins, minerals and fibre, but vegetables are lower in calories and sugar, so guidelines recommend eating more of them. The work combined two large American studies (over 1,00,000 people, followed up to 30 years) with 24 other studies into a meta-analysis of 1.8 million participants.

Variety matters, since different produce supplies different nutrients and antioxidants. Most produce was linked to lower mortality, but fruit juices and starchy vegetables (peas, corn, potatoes) were not — perhaps because of their higher glycaemic load. Fresh, frozen or canned produce all count; freezing and canning preserve nutrients and can make these foods “even more nutrient-dense” than fresh ones, helping people for whom fresh produce is costly or hard to get.

Complete the sentence :
The research study referred to in the given passage claims that the daily consumption of five servings of a variety of fruits and vegetables_________________.
  1. can keep us satisfied and make us immortal.
  2. can lower the risk of diseases and increase life-span.
  3. can make people completely disease free and invincible.
  4. is an age old guideline to cure infertility.
Concept to recallReading comprehension: answer from what the passage says, not from general knowledge; reject options that over-state (always, only, completely) or reverse the text.
  1. The study links five a day to longevity and lower risk of death from heart disease, cancer and respiratory disease.
  2. (1) and (3) exaggerate (immortal, completely, invincible); infertility (4) is never mentioned.

Answer: option (2) — can lower the risk of diseases and increase life-span.

Q53CUET 2023 · 21 May, Shift 1 · Q10NTA final key
Passage (summarised): the early life of Premchand (Q6–10)

A biographical sketch; the paper names no source.

Premchand was born on 31 July 1880 at Lamahi, a village about four miles from Banaras, into a family with some six bighas of land. His grandfather, Gur Sahai Lal, was a patwari; his father, Ajaib Lal, a post-office clerk earning about twenty-five rupees a month. His mother, Anandi Devi, was good-natured and accomplished, reminiscent of the story ‘Barhe Ghar ki Beti’, whose heroine is also called Anandi.

A lively boy with a sweet tooth, he spent his childhood in the village and learnt some Urdu and Persian from a Maulvi Sahib; he was once severely punished for stealing a rupee. His story ‘Kazaki’ draws on childhood memories: Kazaki was a postal messenger who brought the child gifts and was dismissed for delay after chasing a deer for him.

“Premchand” was a pen-name; his real name was Dhanpat Rai. As a government servant he first wrote short stories as Nawab Rai; when the government banned his first collection, Soze Watan, he dropped that name and published everything later as Premchand.

According to the passage, who is responsible for Premchand learning Urdu and Persian?
  1. Yashodanand
  2. Bibijan
  3. Maulvi Sahib
  4. Ramkali
Concept to recallAnswer from what the passage states or clearly implies; reject options that add facts, exaggerate, or are merely silly.
  1. The passage says he had his early schooling at Lamahi, where a Maulvi Sahib taught him some Urdu and Persian.
  2. The other names do not occur in the passage.

Answer: option (3) — Maulvi Sahib

Q54CUET 2023 · 21 May, Shift 1 · Q11NTA final key
Passage (summarised): the entertaining speech (Q11–15)

A note on speech types; it opens with a three-line joke by J. B. Priestley about missing respect both as a youth and as an old man.

A persuasive speech changes mindsets; an informative speech transfers knowledge; an entertaining speech makes speaker and listener feel good about life and themselves. It is light, fun and gracious; toasts, roasts, stand-ups and after-dinner chats are examples. It “sells or promotes happiness and gratitude”, but still needs a good opening, a good closing and a relevant, fun middle, ending on a high note (not necessarily a summary or call to action).

Its elements: several humorous anecdotes about the people involved; dialogue; a light “flip” look at serious things; preferably first person and present tense; quick set-ups and quicker punchlines; varied voice modulation in delivery; and brevity. The speaker should also open up and get close to the audience.

Match List I with List II to complete the information given in the table:
List-IList-II
(A) Persuasive Speech(I) transfers knowledge
(B) Entertaining Speech(II) gives a touch of reality
(C) Informative Speech(III) changes mindsets
(D) Anecdote(IV) makes you feel good
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I
  2. A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I
  3. A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II
  4. A-IV, B-II, C-I, D-III
Concept to recallMatch-the-list: fix the pair you are surest of, then keep only the options that contain it.
  1. Persuasive → changes mindsets (A-III); informative → transfers knowledge (C-I); entertaining → feel good (B-IV).
  2. That leaves anecdote → a touch of reality (a real incident about real people), D-II.

Answer: option (3) — A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

Q63CUET 2023 · 7 Jun, Shift 1 · Q10NTA final key
Passage (summarised): how humans came to walk on two feet (Q6–10)

A popular-science passage; the paper names no source.

Humans are bipedal and use two hands. Bipedalism began in our primate ancestors about 4 million years ago. Primates differ from less evolved mammals in several ways: adaptations to life in trees, big brains, sharper vision, opposable thumbs, and more flexible shoulder movements.

Dr Tetsuro Matsuzawa (Kyoto University) explains that the shared ancestor primates moved into the tree-tops and turned four legs into four hands — an adaptation to “arboreal life” for gripping branches. “Subsequently” early humans left the trees and walked long distances upright, turning four hands into two feet.

Anthropologist Carol Ward (University of Missouri) stresses that our upright, one-foot-after-the-other walking is unique, so it matters to learn how our lineage “diverged” from ape-like creatures.

Our brain is roughly three times the size of a chimpanzee’s, and our cerebral cortex — key to memory, attention, awareness and thought — has twice as many cells. Hence we are smarter than apes.

Which of the following words means the same as 'diverge'
  1. Intersect
  2. Separate
  3. Divulge
  4. Synchronize
Concept to recalldiverge = to separate and go in different directions (opposite: converge).
  1. Our lineage “diverged” from ape-like creatures = separated from them.
  2. Divulge (reveal a secret) is a sound-alike trap; intersect and synchronize imply coming together.

Answer: option (2) — Separate

  1. “Subsequently, early human ancestors left the trees” = later on, they left.

Answer: option (3) — Afterwards

TrapConfusing subsequently (later) with consequently (as a result).
Q67CUET 2023 · 7 Jun, Shift 1 · Q9NTA final key
Passage (summarised): how humans came to walk on two feet (Q6–10)

A popular-science passage; the paper names no source.

Humans are bipedal and use two hands. Bipedalism began in our primate ancestors about 4 million years ago. Primates differ from less evolved mammals in several ways: adaptations to life in trees, big brains, sharper vision, opposable thumbs, and more flexible shoulder movements.

Dr Tetsuro Matsuzawa (Kyoto University) explains that the shared ancestor primates moved into the tree-tops and turned four legs into four hands — an adaptation to “arboreal life” for gripping branches. “Subsequently” early humans left the trees and walked long distances upright, turning four hands into two feet.

Anthropologist Carol Ward (University of Missouri) stresses that our upright, one-foot-after-the-other walking is unique, so it matters to learn how our lineage “diverged” from ape-like creatures.

Our brain is roughly three times the size of a chimpanzee’s, and our cerebral cortex — key to memory, attention, awareness and thought — has twice as many cells. Hence we are smarter than apes.

Which options don't correctly explain why humans are smarter than apes. (as per the passage)
(A) Apes have a bigger brain size.
(B) Humans have a better memory.
(C) Humans can walk with only 2 legs.
(D) Human's ability to process thoughts is more.
(E) Apes can climb trees.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
  1. (A) and (E) Only
  2. (A) and (C) Only
  3. (A), (C) and (E) Only
  4. (C) and (E) Only
Concept to recallAnswer from what the passage states or clearly implies; reject options that add facts, exaggerate, or are merely silly. The passage ties intelligence to brain size and the cerebral cortex (memory, attention, awareness, thought).
  1. (B) and (D) are the passage’s own explanation (cortex for memory and thought), so they are correct explanations.
  2. (A) is false — humans have the bigger brain.
  3. (C) and (E) are true facts from the passage, but walking on two legs and climbing trees say nothing about intelligence. So the options that do not explain it are (A), (C) and (E).

Answer: option (3) — (A), (C) and (E) Only

TrapLeaving out (C): bipedalism is a real human trait in the passage, but the question asks what explains intelligence.
Q68CUET 2023 · 7 Jun, Shift 2 · Q1NTA final key
Passage (summarised): Arabia, the oasis and the desert Arabs

Much of Arabia is desert — only sand and rock, so hot by day that bare feet cannot cross it. Here and there are springs fed from deep underground, too deep for the sun to dry up. They are few and far apart, but around each one tall, graceful trees grow and make a cool, green, shady spot: an oasis.

Desert Arabs live all year in tents that are quickly put up and struck, moving from oasis to oasis to find grass and water for their sheep, goats, camels and horses. They eat ripe figs and the dates of the palm, drying the dates to eat all year.

They own the finest horses in the world; an Arab loves his riding horse almost as much as his wife and children, never loads it heavily and often lets it stay in the family tent.

The camel, however, is far more useful: larger and stronger, it carries as much as two horses or more, and the Arab both loads it with goods and rides it for miles across the desert — which is why it is called the “Ship of the Desert”.

Which of the following is not a part of the geography of the Arab world ?
  1. sand and rock
  2. high mountain ranges
  3. underground springs of water
  4. tall trees
Concept to recall‘Not’ questions: tick off every option the passage mentions; the one left over is the answer.
  1. The passage describes sand and rock, springs from deep underground and tall trees round each oasis.
  2. Mountains are never mentioned — so high mountain ranges is not part of the picture.

Answer: option (2) — high mountain ranges

Trap‘Tall trees’ sounds unlikely for a desert, but the passage places them round every spring.
Q69CUET 2023 · 7 Jun, Shift 2 · Q11NTA final key
Passage (summarised): why the literary life is an unhappy one

The writer argues that a literary life is mostly unhappy. Genius pays its own penalty, and mere talent brings endless cares. There are the “pangs of composition”, the disappointment of an artist who cannot fully express himself, and the constant struggle to win the public’s attention.

Young writers are “buoyed up by the hope” that one poem or novel will win them the laurel crown and instant recognition. They cannot be persuaded that editors and publishers are practical businessmen, “mere brokers” working on profit and loss, not eager to bring good literature to the public. Even a launched book must then face the critics.

Some authors learn to find critics comical and ignore them; sensitive ones are crushed and give up writing. Keats is called the saddest case, his death hastened by the savage attack of Gifford and Terry. Many others suffer “unscrupulous” criticism in silence, because it is a rule of letters that an author must never publicly defend himself: silence is the only safeguard and the only dignified protest against insult.

Why is the literary life mostly an unhappy one -
  1. due to the attitude of the publishers
  2. because of the criticism of the critics
  3. pangs of composition
  4. All of the above
Concept to recallA thesis question: collect every cause the passage lists.
  1. Pangs of composition — listed.
  2. Publishers who are mere profit-minded brokers — listed.
  3. Savage criticism — listed.
  4. Hence all of the above.

Answer: option (4) — All of the above

  1. it is a waterhole
  2. a shallow place
  3. an incubator
  4. a safe and cool shelter
Concept to recallAn oasis is a fertile spot in a desert round a spring or water source — water, shade and refuge.

  1. The Arabs love them as much as they love their wife and children
  2. They are the only means of transport
  3. They are the finest horses in the world
  4. The Arabs never overload their horses
Concept to recallLook for the option the passage contradicts, not just one it fails to mention.
  1. Love for the horse, ‘finest in the world’ and no heavy loads are all stated.
  2. The camel is also ridden and loaded, so horses are clearly not the only means of transport.

Q77CUET 2023 · 10 Jun, Shift 2 · Q1NTA final key
Passage (summarised): community conservation at Kailadevi Wildlife Sanctuary

In most protected areas villagers and forest officials clash, but at the Kailadevi Wildlife Sanctuary in Rajasthan conservation has come from local community initiatives. Set up in 1983 over 674 sq km, it is part of the 1334 sq km Ranthambore Tiger Reserve, in the Karauli and Sapotra blocks of Sawai Madhopur district. The main local communities, the Meenas and Gujjars, live by herding and subsistence farming.

The sanctuary was under pressure from migrant grazers called Rabaris, who came from Mewar with over 150,000 sheep, and from timber and fuelwood cutting and mining. The threat from the migrant grazers led to the “Baragaon ki Panchayat” in 1990, which in turn started the ‘Bhed Bhagao Andolan’ (drive-away-the-sheep movement).

The Forest Department helped villagers form Forest Protection Committees and Van Suraksha Samitis. Local involvement checked illegal felling, regulated local use of forest produce, and the FPCs also stopped mining in the sanctuary. People now protect their forests and use their resources judiciously.

The problem of conservation and regeneration of Kailadevi Wildlife Sanctuary was solved with the initiative of :
  1. Meenas and Gujjars
  2. Local Communities
  3. Forest Officials
  4. State government
Concept to recallMain-idea questions: the answer is the passage’s central claim, usually in its first sentence.
  1. The opening sentence credits ‘local community initiatives’ for conservation and regeneration.

Answer: option (2) — Local Communities

TrapMeenas and Gujjars are among the local people, but the passage credits the community as a whole; the Forest Department only supported it.

Q82CUET 2023 · 15 Jun, Shift 3 · Q1NTA final key
Passage (summarised): water and sleep for teenagers

Since the body is about two-thirds water, staying hydrated matters. The British Nutrition Foundation advises teenagers to drink six to eight glasses of water a day, and more if they play sport or are very active. 100 per cent fruit juice and low-fat milk are other good sources of fluid. Sugary and caffeinated drinks “should be limited or eliminated” from the diet because they give excess sugar and empty calories.

The Cleveland Clinic says teenagers need at least nine hours of sleep a night. That is hard because of early school start times, late-afternoon practices and hours of homework. The advice: keep a regular bedtime that allows nine hours before getting up for school, and plan at least an hour of “quiet time” before bed, with all electronics “to be turned off for the night” so brain and body relax — for example by listening to soothing music or reading a book.

Sports persons need to stay hydrated. They should drink enough :
  1. water and 100% fruit juices
  2. water, milk, coffee
  3. water, juices, tea and coffee
  4. Sugary and caffeinated drinks as well as enough plain water
Concept to recallSeparate what the passage recommends from what it says to limit.
  1. Recommended: water (more for sporty teens), 100% fruit juice, low-fat milk.
  2. Coffee and tea are caffeinated and sugary drinks are to be limited — so (2), (3), (4) fail.

Answer: option (1) — water and 100% fruit juices

Q83CUET 2023 · 15 Jun, Shift 3 · Q10NTA final key
Passage (summarised): preparing to conduct an interview

If you are well prepared, conducting an interview should be “like painting by numbers”. Many aspects benefit from early preparation; left until the candidates arrive, they can harm the process, so a checklist helps make sure nothing, obvious or not, is forgotten.

Often overlooked is the choice of venue and its layout: depending on how the furniture is arranged and how interviewers behave, the room can feel “forbidding”, formal, relaxed or cosy.

Interviews are stressful for candidates and interviewers alike, so this should be considered in the timing of interviews and in briefing the interviewers. Stress also affects how interviewers treat candidates; skill in questioning and in giving candidates information smooths the interview and improves the interviewers’ performance (and helps managers elsewhere too). Even the way the interview ends can influence whether the chosen candidate accepts the job offer.

Which of the following could be a suitable title for the passage ?
  1. How to conduct an Interview
  2. How to give an Interview
  3. An Introduction to Interviews
  4. How to get a Job
Concept to recallA title names the topic and the angle (here: advice to interviewers).
  1. The whole passage advises the interviewer on preparation → How to conduct an interview.

Answer: option (1) — How to conduct an Interview

Trap‘Give an interview’ and ‘get a job’ are the candidate’s angle.

  2. (A), (B), (C) and (D)
  3. (B), (C) and (D) only
  4. (A), (B) and (C) only
Concept to recallFine distinctions in option wording: match the passage’s exact claim (‘all electronics … for the night’).
  1. The passage: at least an hour of quiet time before bed (C), all electronics turned off for the night (B).
  2. (A) is weaker than what is said, and (D) adds a ‘place’ that is not mentioned.

Answer: option (1) — (B) and (C) only

Q86CUET 2023 · 15 Jun, Shift 3 · Q4NTA final key
Passage (summarised): water and sleep for teenagers

Since the body is about two-thirds water, staying hydrated matters. The British Nutrition Foundation advises teenagers to drink six to eight glasses of water a day, and more if they play sport or are very active. 100 per cent fruit juice and low-fat milk are other good sources of fluid. Sugary and caffeinated drinks “should be limited or eliminated” from the diet because they give excess sugar and empty calories.

The Cleveland Clinic says teenagers need at least nine hours of sleep a night. That is hard because of early school start times, late-afternoon practices and hours of homework. The advice: keep a regular bedtime that allows nine hours before getting up for school, and plan at least an hour of “quiet time” before bed, with all electronics “to be turned off for the night” so brain and body relax — for example by listening to soothing music or reading a book.

Choose the heading that best explains the two sections in the text given :
(A) Watch your beverage intake
(B) Eat right, sleep tight
(C) If you don’t snooze, you lose
(D) Making time for friends
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
  1. (A) and (C) only
  2. (A) and (B) only
  3. (B) and (C) only
  4. (B) and (D) only
Concept to recallA heading must fit its section’s topic exactly: section 1 = drinks, section 2 = sleep.
  1. Section 1 is about what to drink → (A).
  2. Section 2 is about sleep → (C).
  3. ‘Eat right’ is about food, which the passage does not discuss.

Answer: option (1) — (A) and (C) only

Q87CUET 2023 · 15 Jun, Shift 3 · Q6NTA final key
Passage (summarised): preparing to conduct an interview

If you are well prepared, conducting an interview should be “like painting by numbers”. Many aspects benefit from early preparation; left until the candidates arrive, they can harm the process, so a checklist helps make sure nothing, obvious or not, is forgotten.

Often overlooked is the choice of venue and its layout: depending on how the furniture is arranged and how interviewers behave, the room can feel “forbidding”, formal, relaxed or cosy.

Interviews are stressful for candidates and interviewers alike, so this should be considered in the timing of interviews and in briefing the interviewers. Stress also affects how interviewers treat candidates; skill in questioning and in giving candidates information smooths the interview and improves the interviewers’ performance (and helps managers elsewhere too). Even the way the interview ends can influence whether the chosen candidate accepts the job offer.

Who is the intended audience of the passage ?
  1. Job applicants
  2. Students
  3. Teachers
  4. Interviewers
Concept to recallAudience: ask whom the advice is addressed to — who would act on it?
  1. The advice is on preparing venue, timing, briefing and questioning — things the people conducting interviews do.

Answer: option (4) — Interviewers

TrapCandidates are discussed, but the passage is not written for them.

Q90CUET 2023 · 18 Jun, Shift 1 · Q10NTA final key

Organisms change over time; some changes do not affect survival, others do. The example is a group of antelopes in which one animal has longer legs than its siblings. Choose an appropriate title for the passage from the following options:-
  1. Adaptation and Mutation
  2. Mutation: A Necessity
  3. Genetic Code
  4. Survival of the Antelope
Concept to recallA title must cover the whole passage, not one example or one detail.
  1. Paragraph 1 is about adaptation (antelope legs); paragraph 2 is about mutation.
  2. “Survival of the Antelope” is only the example; “Genetic Code” is one detail; “A Necessity” is contradicted (many mutations give no advantage).

Answer: option (1) — Adaptation and Mutation

Q91CUET 2023 · 18 Jun, Shift 1 · Q11NTA final key
Passage (summarised): why we use paper money (Q11–15)

Paying Rs 100 in nickel or copper coins would be heavy and slow to count, so the Government allows payment in rupee notes. These are real money though made of paper: they are lighter to carry and save scarce silver and other metals.

A note is worth the number printed on it because the Government guarantees to pay that amount to anyone who wants to exchange it for coins; without notes, crores more coins would have to be minted.

Why not paper only? Because money must be something everyone wants, because metals are the best form of money, and because it is impossible to print exactly the right amount of paper money. If a Government prints too much, prices go up at once and the value of money falls — money is useful only for what it buys, so the more money there is, the higher prices become. Paper is easy to print in excess; metal’s steady supply is one chief reason coins were chosen.

The Government allows payment to be made in __________
  1. nickel
  2. rupee coins
  3. copper coins
  4. rupee notes
Concept to recallAnswer from what the passage states; reject options that are true in general but not said there.
  1. Coins are heavy and slow to count, so the Government “permits you to make the payment in rupee-notes”.
  2. The coins are what the notes replace for convenience.

Answer: option (4) — rupee notes

Q99CUET 2023 · 19 Jun, Shift 2 · Q11NTA final key
Passage (summarised): where knowledge is found (Q11–15)

Knowledge takes many forms and is found in many places. It is acquired through education, information, intelligence and experience, and is available in academic institutions, with teachers, in libraries and research papers, and in workplaces — with workers and managers, in drawings, process sheets and on shop floors.

Though linked to education, knowledge comes equally from the skills of artists, craftsmen, traditional healers, philosophers, saints and housewives, and it shapes their work. Our heritage and history — rituals, epics and traditions that are part of our consciousness — are vast resources of knowledge, as are libraries and universities. Villages hold much unorthodox, earthy wisdom, and there are hidden treasures of knowledge in oceans, bioreserves, deserts and plant and animal life. Every state of the country has a unique core competence for a knowledge society.

How is knowledge acquired according to the author ?
  1. Through learning and applying concepts
  2. By getting skills and information
  3. Through hard work and sincerity
  4. By toiling day and night
Concept to recallAnswer from what the passage states; reject options that are true in general but not said there.
  1. The passage: knowledge is acquired through education, information, intelligence and experience.
  2. NTA keys (1): education and experience amount to learning and applying what is learnt.
  3. (3) and (4) speak of effort, which the passage never mentions.

Answer: option (1) — Through learning and applying concepts

NoteNTA’s final key accepts both (1) and (2); option (2) echoes the passage’s own words (skills, information). Either earned the marks.

Q104CUET 2023 · 21 Jun, Shift 1 · Q10NTA final key
Passage (summarised): values and Indian roots in the curriculum (from India’s National Education Policy 2020)

Children will be taught early the importance of “doing what’s right” and given a logical framework for ethical decisions, later extended to themes such as cheating, violence, plagiarism, littering, tolerance, equality and empathy. Basic human and Constitutional values — among them seva, ahimsa, swachchhata, satya, nishkam karma, shanti, sacrifice, tolerance, diversity, respect for elders and the environment, helpfulness, courtesy, patience, empathy, compassion, patriotism, and democratic values such as justice, liberty, equality and fraternity — will be developed in all students. They will read Panchatantra, Jataka and Hitopadesha tales, excerpts from the Constitution, and get basic training in health, hygiene, first-aid and the harm done by alcohol, tobacco and drugs.

From the foundational stage, all curriculum and pedagogy will be redesigned to be rooted in the Indian and local context and “ethos” — culture, traditions, heritage, language, philosophy, geography, indigenous ways of learning — so that education is “maximally relatable, relevant, interesting, and effective”; ideas, abstractions and creativity flourish best when learning is so rooted.

Which of the following are not constitutional values ?
(A) swachchhata
(B) satya
(C) ashanti
(D) seva
(E) himsa
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (C) and (E) only
  2. (A) and (B) only
  3. (B) and (E) only
  4. (C) and (D) only
Concept to recallThe prefix a- in Sanskrit negates: ahimsa = non-violence, a-shanti = unrest.
  1. The list has shanti (peace) and ahimsa (non-violence).
  2. ashanti (unrest) and himsa (violence) are their opposites, so (C) and (E) are not values.

Answer: option (1) — (C) and (E) only

TrapThe negating prefix sits on the other word in each pair.
Q105CUET 2023 · 21 Jun, Shift 1 · Q11NTA final key
Passage (summarised): water pollution

Water pollution — the addition or presence of undesirable substances in water — is one of the most serious environmental problems. Human causes are industrial, agricultural and domestic: farm run-off laden with fertilisers and pesticides, industrial effluents with toxic substances, and sewage with human and animal wastes. Natural causes are soil erosion, leaching of minerals from rocks and decaying organic matter.

Rivers, lakes, seas, estuaries and ground water may be polluted by point or non-point sources. Point source pollution comes from one specific location, such as a drain pipe discharging industrial effluents directly into a water body. Non-point sources are diffuse: run-off from farms, grazing land, construction sites, abandoned mines, pits, roads and streets.

What represents point source pollution ?
  1. Drain pipe carrying industrial effluents discharged directly into a water body
  2. River and seas getting polluted by washing activities
  3. Discharge of pollutants from diffused sources
  4. Decaying of organic matter
Concept to recallPoint source = a single identifiable outlet; non-point = diffuse run-off.
  1. The passage’s own example of a point source is the drain pipe carrying effluents.
  2. (3) is the definition of non-point sources; (4) is a natural cause.

Answer: option (1) — Drain pipe carrying industrial effluents discharged directly into a water body

Non-point sources are diffuse: run-off from farms, grazing land, construction sites, abandoned mines, pits, roads and streets.

Addition or presence of undesirable substances in water is called :
  1. Noise pollution
  2. Water pollution
  3. Soil pollution
  4. Air pollution
Concept to recallThe passage opens with this definition.
  1. Undesirable substances in water = water pollution.

Answer: option (2) — Water pollution

Q108CUET 2023 · 21 Jun, Shift 1 · Q14NTA final key
Passage (summarised): water pollution

Water pollution — the addition or presence of undesirable substances in water — is one of the most serious environmental problems. Human causes are industrial, agricultural and domestic: farm run-off laden with fertilisers and pesticides, industrial effluents with toxic substances, and sewage with human and animal wastes. Natural causes are soil erosion, leaching of minerals from rocks and decaying organic matter.

Rivers, lakes, seas, estuaries and ground water may be polluted by point or non-point sources. Point source pollution comes from one specific location, such as a drain pipe discharging industrial effluents directly into a water body. Non-point sources are diffuse: run-off from farms, grazing land, construction sites, abandoned mines, pits, roads and streets.

Which is not the natural sources of water pollution ?
  1. Soil Erosion
  2. Leaching of minerals from rocks
  3. Decaying of organic matter
  4. Smoke from cars
Concept to recallThe passage’s three natural sources: soil erosion, leaching of minerals, decaying organic matter.
  1. Options (1)–(3) are exactly those three.
  2. Car smoke is man-made (and mainly an air pollutant).

Answer: option (4) — Smoke from cars

  1. The passage lists rivers, lakes, seas, oceans, estuaries and ground water as open to pollution from ‘point or non-point sources’.

Q110CUET 2023 · 21 Jun, Shift 1 · Q6NTA final key
Passage (summarised): values and Indian roots in the curriculum (from India’s National Education Policy 2020)

Children will be taught early the importance of “doing what’s right” and given a logical framework for ethical decisions, later extended to themes such as cheating, violence, plagiarism, littering, tolerance, equality and empathy. Basic human and Constitutional values — among them seva, ahimsa, swachchhata, satya, nishkam karma, shanti, sacrifice, tolerance, diversity, respect for elders and the environment, helpfulness, courtesy, patience, empathy, compassion, patriotism, and democratic values such as justice, liberty, equality and fraternity — will be developed in all students. They will read Panchatantra, Jataka and Hitopadesha tales, excerpts from the Constitution, and get basic training in health, hygiene, first-aid and the harm done by alcohol, tobacco and drugs.

From the foundational stage, all curriculum and pedagogy will be redesigned to be rooted in the Indian and local context and “ethos” — culture, traditions, heritage, language, philosophy, geography, indigenous ways of learning — so that education is “maximally relatable, relevant, interesting, and effective”; ideas, abstractions and creativity flourish best when learning is so rooted.

Why do we need to redesign all curriculum and pedagogy in terms of culture, heritage and traditions at a foundational level ?
  1. to ensure maximisation of national pride
  2. to avoid the damaging and detrimental effects of global learning
  3. to ensure that education is maximally relatable, relevant and interesting for students
  4. to ensure that ideas, abstraction and creativity are confined to higher educations
Concept to recallFind the purpose clause (‘in order to ensure that …’).
  1. The passage: ‘in order to ensure that education is maximally relatable, relevant, interesting, and effective’.
  2. National pride and ‘harm of global learning’ are not stated; (4) contradicts ‘creativity flourishes’ when learning is rooted.

Answer: option (3) — to ensure that education is maximally relatable, relevant and interesting for students

Select an appropriate title for the passage from the following options :
  1. The Future of Pedagogy

  1. intolerance

Q113CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 2 · Q6NTA final key
Passage (summarised): children in a digital world

Digital technology — the internet, tablets, smartphones, social media and messaging — has changed childhood: it has transformed young people’s education and learning, how they make and keep friends, their leisure and their engagement with society. UNICEF’s State of the World’s Children 2017 found that one in three internet users is under 18 and 71% of 15–24-year-olds are online. But the digital divide is large: 346 million youth are not online, with African adolescents worst hit (60% not connected, against 4% in Europe). Youth who lack digital skills, live in remote regions or speak a minority language are also left behind.

The flip side: cyberbullying lets bullies hurt and humiliate victims with a click, and harmful posts are hard to delete, raising the risk of re-victimisation. Moderate use helps mental wellbeing, but excessive use can be “detrimental”; social relationships seem enhanced; evidence on physical activity is mixed.

Popularity will keep growing, yet there is an intergenerational gap in digital literacy, so teachers and parents need training. Schools should tackle online harassment, and children must be the priority of digital policy, both for protection and so technology helps them reach their potential.

How has the Digital technologies affected the lives of youth around the world ?
  1. It has made education and learning more accessible.
  2. It has not changed the way they make and maintain friendships.
  3. It has eradicated Bullying
  4. It has increased the time youth spend outdoors
Concept to recallAnswer from the passage’s own claim: technology has ‘transformed their education and learning’.
  1. The passage says digital tools transformed education and learning — option (1).
  2. (2) contradicts ‘the way they make and maintain friendship’ being transformed.
  3. (3) is the opposite: bullying moved online. (4): physical-activity evidence is only ‘mixed’.

Answer: option (1) — It has made education and learning more accessible.

Select the correct option from the following list :
(A) 346 million youth are online
(B) young people who lack digital skills, mostly line in remote regions.
(C) one in three internet users is younger than 18 years.
(D) 60% adolescents in Africa and 4% in Europe are not connected to the Internet.
(E) 75% of 15-24 year olds are online.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (A), (C) and (D) only
  2. (A) and (E) only
  3. (B) only
  4. (E) only
Concept to recallCheck each figure against the passage: 346 million are not online; 71% (not 75%) of 15–24s are online.
  1. (C) and (D) are correct as stated.
  2. (A) is wrong strictly (the 346 million are not online) and (E) misquotes 71% as 75%.
  3. (B) loosely restates the passage’s list of the left-behind (lacking skills, remote regions).

Answer: option (1) — (A), (C) and (D) only

NoteNTA’s final key accepts both (1) and (3): (1) contains the misquoted (A), and (B) is only a loose paraphrase. Either earned marks.

Which of the following statements is correct ?
  1. An intergenerational gap doesn’t emist in digital knowledge and literacy
  2. Moderate use of digital technology can be beneficial to children’s mental well being
  3. Excessive use of digital technology can be beneficial to children’s mental well being
  4. The popularity of digital technologies is on the decline
Concept to recallTrue/false items: one word (moderate/excessive, exists/doesn’t) flips a statement.

Q116CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q10NTA final key
Passage (summarised): building the Channel Tunnel

In 1984 France and Britain agreed that a link across the English Channel would benefit both and create jobs, but neither government could pay for so huge a project, so they held a contest. Entrants had to give a plan to raise the funds, be able to operate the link once built, and make it last at least 120 years.

Ten proposals came in, tunnels and bridges among them. Some were so “outlandish” they were easily dismissed; others too expensive ever to be finished. The winner planned two parallel railway tunnels under the Channel, with a third, smaller tunnel between them for maintenance (drainage pipes, communication cables and so on). After the first test run on 10 December 1993, the Channel Tunnel officially opened on 6 May 1994.

Which of the following statement is incorrect with respect to the given passage ?
  1. The smaller tunnel was to be used to provide a passage for aquatic animals.
  2. Shuttles would be able to hold cars and trucks.
  3. Some trains would carry passengers only.
  4. Most of the proposal to build the link were rejected.
Concept to recallThe service tunnel’s stated purpose: maintenance, drainage pipes, communication cables.
  1. The third tunnel is for maintenance — nothing about aquatic animals, so (1) is incorrect.
  2. Nine of ten proposals were rejected (4). (2) and (3) describe the tunnel’s actual services and are not contradicted.

Answer: option (1) — The smaller tunnel was to be used to provide a passage for aquatic animals.
