After the first test run on 10 December 1993, the Channel Tunnel officially opened on 6 May 1994.

What did the context involving the competing companies require ? Choose the incorrect option.
  1. The companies were supposed to provide a plan to raise the needed funds to build the project.
  2. The companies were expected to operate the proposed channel link once the project was completed.
  3. The link across the English Channel was supposed to be outlandish. The companies were asked to keep that in mind.
  4. The link must be able to endure for at least 120 years.
Concept to recall‘Incorrect’ questions: find the option that misuses a word from the passage.
  1. Funding plan, operating the link and a 120-year life were the three requirements.
  2. ‘Outlandish’ described proposals that were rejected; it was never a requirement.

Answer: option (3) — The link across the English Channel was supposed to be outlandish. The companies were asked to keep that in mind.

  1. 6 May, 1994
  2. 10 December, 1993
  3. 6 August, 1993
  4. 11 December, 1994

  1. The test run came first, on 10 December 1993.
  2. 6 May 1994 is the official opening.

Answer: option (2) — 10 December, 1993

Q119CUET 2023 · 2 Jul, Shift 3 · Q11NTA final key
Passage (summarised): will our species last?

No species lasts forever. Ours has existed for at least 200,000 years, which is not old in evolutionary terms, so we should “persist” for hundreds of thousands of years more, and there is no sign that Homo sapiens is in decline. Whether we could destroy ourselves completely — by nuclear annihilation, say — is debated; some argue humans are so numerous, widespread and adaptable that no single catastrophe would wipe us out.

A collapse of global ecosystems caused by climate change and overpopulation has also been predicted as a route to our extinction, but it is hard to believe it could cause a human die-off everywhere. It is impossible to “predict” the coming centuries; yet, more than any other species, humanity can steer its own evolution through technology, genetic modification and control of resources, which makes it likely we will outlast the typical mammal species.

Which of the following sentences are factually incorrect as per the passage?
(A) Our species is 200,000 years old
(B) Our species is not old in evolutionary terms
(C) Our species is in decline
(D) Our species can become extinct due to overpopulation
(E) Our species is unable to control its evolution
Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below
  1. A, B and C only
  2. B and D only
  3. A, D and E only
  4. C and E only
Concept to recall‘Incorrect’ = contradicted by the passage, not merely loosely worded.
  1. (C) is contradicted: ‘no indications that Homo sapiens is in decline’.
  2. (E) is contradicted: humanity is able to control its evolution.
  3. (A) (‘at least’ 200,000), (B) and (D) (a predicted cause) agree with the passage.

Answer: option (4) — C and E only

Q122CUET 2022 · 16 Sep, Shift 1 · Set 42 · Q13key re-derived
Passage (summarised): the sickness of spirit (Q13–18)

A philosophical essay; the paper names no source.

Unhappiness and discontent come not only from poverty. The author calls man a strange creature, fundamentally different from the other animals, with far horizons, invincible hopes, creative energies and spiritual powers; if these stay undeveloped and unsatisfied, he may have every comfort wealth can give and still feel life is not worthwhile.

The celebrated humanist writers — Shaw, Wells, Arnold Bennett and Galsworthy, called “the prophets of the dawn” — expose the weaknesses of modern life but ignore its deeper currents and put nothing in their place. The modern mind has been shaped by Rousseau’s Social Contract, Marx, Darwin and Spengler; our outer chaos reflects the confusion in our minds, and (quoting Plato) constitutions mirror the values in men’s minds.

Ideals and values must change before society can. What our age lacks is the soul; we suffer from “sickness of spirit” and must regain faith in a transcendent truth that brings unity and purpose. Otherwise, when floods and winds beat upon our house, “it will fall”.

The author implies that if the eternal values and ideals are not regained then ______
(Select the right option)
  1. The world will be flooded
  2. The sky will fall
  3. The human civilization and society will be ruined forever
  4. The earth will get sucked into a black hole
Concept to recallInference from metaphor: the closing “floods … winds … it will fall” is a figurative warning, not a forecast.
  1. The house that falls in the storm stands for our civilisation built without spiritual foundations.
  2. So the implication is that society will be ruined.
  3. Reading the image literally gives the flood/sky distractors; a black hole is pure invention.

Answer: option (3) — The human civilization and society will be ruined forever

  2. “Religion and rituals” is narrower (rituals are never mentioned); material welfare is the thing the author says is not enough.

Answer: option (1) — The spiritual aspect of life

A philosophical essay; the paper names no source.

Unhappiness and discontent come not only from poverty. The author calls man a strange creature, fundamentally different from the other animals, with far horizons, invincible hopes, creative energies and spiritual powers; if these stay undeveloped and unsatisfied, he may have every comfort wealth can give and still feel life is not worthwhile.

The celebrated humanist writers — Shaw, Wells, Arnold Bennett and Galsworthy, called “the prophets of the dawn” — expose the weaknesses of modern life but ignore its deeper currents and put nothing in their place. The modern mind has been shaped by Rousseau’s Social Contract, Marx, Darwin and Spengler; our outer chaos reflects the confusion in our minds, and (quoting Plato) constitutions mirror the values in men’s minds.

Ideals and values must change before society can. What our age lacks is the soul; we suffer from “sickness of spirit” and must regain faith in a transcendent truth that brings unity and purpose. Otherwise, when floods and winds beat upon our house, “it will fall”.

Match List I with List II
List-IList-II
(A) The strange creature man(I) Social Contract
(B) Prophets of dawn are(II) Spiritual development
(C) The famous book written by Rousseau(III) is fundamentally different from other animals
(D) Our age is missing out on(IV) Shaw and Wells, Arnold and Galsworthy
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. A - III, B - IV, C - I, D - II
  2. A - I, B - II, C - III, D - IV
  3. A - II, B - III, C - IV, D - I
  4. A - IV, B - III, C - II, D - I
Concept to recallMatch-the-list: fix the pair you are surest of, then keep only the options that contain it.
  1. Rousseau → Social Contract: C-I. Only the first option has C-I.
  2. Check: man is fundamentally different (A-III), the prophets of the dawn are Shaw, Wells, Bennett, Galsworthy (B-IV), our age misses the soul — spiritual development (D-II).

Answer: option (1) — A - III, B - IV, C - I, D - II

Q127CUET 2022 · 16 Sep, Shift 1 · Set 42 · Q18key re-derived
Passage (summarised): the sickness of spirit (Q13–18)

A philosophical essay; the paper names no source.

Unhappiness and discontent come not only from poverty. The modern mind has been shaped by Rousseau’s Social Contract, Marx, Darwin and Spengler; our outer chaos reflects the confusion in our minds, and (quoting Plato) constitutions mirror the values in men’s minds.

Despite enjoying all comforts that wealth can provide, man will still feel incomplete and unhappy if ______
(Select the right option)
  1. He is prevented from mingling in the society
  2. His hopes, creative energies and spiritual powers are unsatisfied
  3. He is deserted by his friends
  4. He had failed to enroll in a Central University in India
Concept to recallAnswer from what the passage states or clearly implies; reject options that add facts, exaggerate, or are merely silly.
  1. If these powers are left “undeveloped and unsatisfied”, man may have every comfort of wealth and still feel that life is “not worthwhile”.
  2. “They” = his hopes, creative energies and spiritual powers. Society, friends and universities are not mentioned.

Answer: option (2) — His hopes, creative energies and spiritual powers are unsatisfied

Reading Comprehension: Narrative and Literary Passages121 questions

Q128CUET 2026 · 11 May, Shift 1 · Q46NTA final key
Passage (summarised): the century-old house (Q46–50)

Summary in our own words; the exam printed the full extract.

The narrator’s elder brother, then 95, phoned him from Rameswaram. He told how the narrator’s friend had visited and asked the age of the house. The brother said their father had built it more than a century ago, and that the younger brother and the earning grandchildren now proposed to demolish it and build a new house on the same site.

The friend did not want “such a historical place demolished”. He offered to arrange, through a trust, to turn the house into a museum and library, while other accommodation was found for the brother’s family.

The brother had called to say he was against the proposal: he wanted to live where he had lived for 95 years, and to build the new house on the same land with the earnings of his “kith and kin”; the narrator should thank the friend politely. “It struck me”, says the narrator, that here was a man who wanted to live on his own terms and take no help, however well meant. He saw in his brother a reflection of their father, who lived to 103.

Choose the best option to complete the sentence:
From the offer made by the narrator's friend, it's evident that the friend is-
  1. greedy
  2. an opportunist
  3. a Romanist
  4. an Antiquarian
Concept to recallAntiquarian = one who values and preserves old, historical things.
  1. He wanted to save a century-old “historical place” as a museum and library.
  2. He gains nothing – not greedy or an opportunist; “Romanist” (a Roman Catholic, or a scholar of Rome) has no basis.

Answer: option (4) — an Antiquarian

Trap“Opportunist” tempts if one reads the offer cynically; the passage calls it well-meant.

He saw in his brother a reflection of their father, who lived to 103.

Which among the following was not a topic of conversation between the narrator and his elder brother?
  1. Buying a new house for the narrator
  2. Transforming the house into a museum
  3. Transforming the house into a library
  4. Making arrangements through a trust
Concept to recall“NOT” question: three options come from the friend’s proposal; find the odd one.
  1. Museum, library and the trust are all in the proposal the brother described.
  2. The new house was to be built for the brother’s family on the same land, not bought for the narrator.

Answer: option (1) — Buying a new house for the narrator

Q130CUET 2026 · 11 May, Shift 1 · Q48NTA final key
Passage (summarised): the century-old house (Q46–50)

Summary in our own words; the exam printed the full extract.

The brother said their father had built it more than a century ago, and that the younger brother and the earning grandchildren now proposed to demolish it and build a new house on the same site.

He saw in his brother a reflection of their father, who lived to 103.

Choose the correct option to complete the sentence-
The narrator’s friend did not want the house to be demolished because it was ________.
  1. a magnificent building
  2. a historical building
  3. an architectural marvel
  4. a newly constructed building
Concept to recallUse the friend’s own words: he would not like to see “such a historical place demolished”.
  1. Built by their father more than a century ago ⇒ historical.
  2. Magnificence or architecture are never mentioned; it is old, not new.

Answer: option (2) — a historical building

Q131CUET 2026 · 6 Jun, Shift 1 · Q46NTA final key
Passage (summarised): Tao Ying on the bus (Q46–50)

Summary in our own words; the exam printed the full extract of a short story.

When Tao Ying rides the bus alone she often does not buy a ticket, reasoning that the bus, its crew and its fuel cost the same with or without her. She is “astute”: if the conductor looks responsible she buys a ticket at once; if he seems careless, she does not pay, treating it as a small punishment for him and a small saving for herself.

She is a cook in a factory canteen and spends all day beside an open fire baking wheat cakes.

Today her son Xiao Ye is with her. Her jacket catches in the closing door and she wriggles free. “Mama, tickets!” says Xiao Ye – children, the narrator notes, are more conscious of rituals than adults; without a ticket the ride does not feel proper to him. A painted finger on the door marks a height of 1.10 m.

The boy’s hair looks “as fluffy as a bundle of straw”, dry and dull. Tao Ying is “very careful with her purse”, but has “never skimped on her child’s diet”; he is healthy and clever, though his hair is a mess.

Which of the following does not hold true for the protagonist of the story?
  1. She is a law abiding citizen.
  2. She is astute.
  3. Plentitude is her second name.
  4. She works in highly conducive environment.
Concept to recall“Does not hold true”: check each statement; only one is directly supported by the passage.
  1. She skips buying tickets ⇒ not law-abiding (statement 1 is false).
  2. “Clearly Tao Ying has to be astute” ⇒ statement 2 is true.
  3. She is careful with money (not “plenitude”), and works all day by an open fire (not conducive) ⇒ 3 and 4 are false too.

Answer: option (1) — She is a law abiding citizen.

NoteNTA’s final key accepts options 1, 3 and 4; all three are untrue of her. Only (2) is true.
Q132CUET 2026 · 6 Jun, Shift 1 · Q47NTA final key
Passage (summarised): Tao Ying on the bus (Q46–50)

Summary in our own words; the exam printed the full extract of a short story.

When Tao Ying rides the bus alone she often does not buy a ticket, reasoning that the bus, its crew and its fuel cost the same with or without her. She is “astute”: if the conductor looks responsible she buys a ticket at once; if he seems careless, she does not pay, treating it as a small punishment for him and a small saving for herself.

Her jacket catches in the closing door and she wriggles free. “Mama, tickets!” says Xiao Ye – children, the narrator notes, are more conscious of rituals than adults; without a ticket the ride does not feel proper to him. A painted finger on the door marks a height of 1.10 m.

The boy’s hair looks “as fluffy as a bundle of straw”, dry and dull. Tao Ying is “very careful with her purse”, but has “never skimped on her child’s diet”; he is healthy and clever, though his hair is a mess.

'She has never skimped on her child's diet' clearly states that:
  1. She is a strict mother.
  2. She wants to save on eatables.
  3. She is careful about her child's nutritive requirements.
  4. She takes her maternal duties for granted.
Concept to recallSkimp on = spend too little on. Never skimping = always providing enough.
  1. Though thrifty, she spends freely on his food ⇒ careful about his nutrition.
  2. Option 2 says the opposite; strictness and taking duties for granted are not stated.

Answer: option (3) — She is careful about her child's nutritive requirements.

Q133CUET 2026 · 6 Jun, Shift 1 · Q48NTA final key
Passage (summarised): Tao Ying on the bus (Q46–50)

Her jacket catches in the closing door and she wriggles free. “Mama, tickets!” says Xiao Ye – children, the narrator notes, are more conscious of rituals than adults; without a ticket the ride does not feel proper to him. A painted finger on the door marks a height of 1.10 m.

The boy’s hair looks “as fluffy as a bundle of straw”, dry and dull. Tao Ying is “very careful with her purse”, but has “never skimped on her child’s diet”; he is healthy and clever, though his hair is a mess.

Tao Ying's son's concern about the ticket shows that children, compared to adults, are :
  1. lackadaisical
  2. reckless
  3. conscientious
  4. dexterous
Concept to recallConscientious = careful to do what is right. The narrator says children are more conscious of rituals than adults.
  1. “Mama, tickets!” – the boy insists on doing it properly ⇒ conscientious.
  2. Lackadaisical (careless) and reckless are opposites; dexterous = skilful with hands.

Answer: option (3) — conscientious

Q134CUET 2025 · 13 May, Shift 1 · Q1NTA final key
Passage (summarised): Miss Stubbs (Q1–4)

Summary in our own words; the exam printed the full extract.

The narrator, a visitor (the vet), sits by the bed of the old invalid Miss Stubbs while her helper Mrs. Broadwith brings tea and lets the animals in from the kitchen, as on many earlier visits. Asked how she is, Miss Stubbs says she is much better and at once changes the subject.

She mostly talks about her pets, past and present, going back to her girlhood, and about the days when her family was alive. She loves to describe the “escapades of her three brothers”, shows a photograph of them, laughs that they were “young rips”, and her face briefly lights up.

The narrator recalls village gossip: the family was once prosperous and lived in the big house, but foreign investments crashed and the father died almost penniless – “There is not much brass there now.” There is probably just enough brass left to feed her and her animals and to pay Mrs. Broadwith. The narrator feels the weight of his responsibility; the only light in the brave old woman’s life is the devotion of her animals, whose eyes never leave her face.

Miss Stubbs led a very simple life because ______.
  1. she didn't believe in leading a luxurious life
  2. She was too sad a person to enjoy simple pleasures of life
  3. she couldn't afford even the normal little luxuries
  4. she was bed-ridden and bitter about it
Concept to recallInference from the narrator’s background: the family fortune was lost (“not much brass there now”).
  1. The villagers say the father died “almost penniless”; there is “probably just enough brass” to keep her and her animals alive.
  2. So her simple life is forced by poverty, not chosen ⇒ she could not afford even small luxuries.
  3. Not a belief (no hint of principle); not sad or bitter – her face is “radiant” and she is called “brave”.

Answer: option (3) — she couldn't afford even the normal little luxuries

Trap“Bed-ridden” is half true (the card above her bed) but “bitter” contradicts the cheerful talk.
Q135CUET 2025 · 13 May, Shift 1 · Q2NTA final key
Passage (summarised): Miss Stubbs (Q1–4)

Summary in our own words; the exam printed the full extract.

The narrator, a visitor (the vet), sits by the bed of the old invalid Miss Stubbs while her helper Mrs. Broadwith brings tea and lets the animals in from the kitchen, as on many earlier visits. Asked how she is, Miss Stubbs says she is much better and at once changes the subject.

The narrator feels the weight of his responsibility; the only light in the brave old woman’s life is the devotion of her animals, whose eyes never leave her face.

Which among the following was not a topic of Miss Stubb's conversation?
  1. her brothers
  2. her pets
  3. her past with her family
  4. her classmates
Concept to recall“NOT” questions: tick off each option against the passage; the one never mentioned is the answer.
  1. Pets – “she liked to talk about her pets”.
  2. Brothers – “the escapades of her three brothers”.
  3. Family past – “the days her family was alive”.
  4. Classmates are never mentioned.

Answer: option (4) — her classmates

Trap“Back to her girlhood” tempts one to imagine school friends; the passage speaks only of pets from that time.
Q136CUET 2025 · 13 May, Shift 1 · Q5NTA final key
Passage (summarised): born to dance (Q5–8)

Summary in our own words; the exam printed the full extract.

The narrator, Kumudini, says her younger self would be “incredulous” to see her now: that she works in dance, decoding it for herself – “call it choreography if you wish” – would have seemed unbelievable. She envies dancers who claim to be “born to dance”, but finds the claim doubtful: it is rarely that easy, and for her “‘To dance’ means ‘to struggle’”.

As a child she never wanted to dance; it was forced on her by a doting mother and a silent father, who “probably kept his peace to avoid argument”. The lessons were hard, harder for her mother, who took a tired, unwilling child by crowded local train after school.

At seven, after a film in which Mumtaz Ali danced, she pranced round the house imitating him; her mother, watching quietly, declared that she was born to dance. The narrator does not remember this; it was her mother who saw the innate ability in her.

The narrator's younger self would be incredulous if she saw the narrator now, as:
  1. she had become a choreographer.
  2. she couldn't decipher the nuances of dance.
  3. she was too curious to learn dance since her early childhood.
  4. her reality and her dreams were not bridged.
Concept to recallIncredulous = unable to believe something. Find what would have seemed unbelievable.
  1. She says her younger self would have found it unbelievable that she now works in dance, as a choreographer.
  2. So the child would not believe she became a choreographer.
  3. Option 3 contradicts “I never did want to dance”; option 2 contradicts “decipher and translate dance”.

Answer: option (1) — she had become a choreographer.

TrapOption 4 is a roundabout restatement; NTA accepted it as well.
NoteNTA’s final key accepts both (1) and (4): the child never wanted to dance, so what she became did not match what she dreamed of. (1) is the direct reading.
Q137CUET 2025 · 13 May, Shift 1 · Q6NTA final key
Passage (summarised): born to dance (Q5–8)

Summary in our own words; the exam printed the full extract.

At seven, after a film in which Mumtaz Ali danced, she pranced round the house imitating him; her mother, watching quietly, declared that she was born to dance. The narrator does not remember this; it was her mother who saw the innate ability in her.

The narrator says,'to dance means to struggle' as she ______.
  1. was envious of the other dancers' talent.
  2. had tough time convincing her parents about her passion
  3. doesn't have good memories of her childhood
  4. had to work hard to perfect the art, though unwillingly
Concept to recallConnect the claim to the evidence that follows it: dance was forced on her, lessons under trying conditions.
  1. She doubts dancers “born to dance”: “it is rarely that easy”.
  2. Her own case: dance was forced on her; lessons “under trying conditions”, as an unwilling child.
  3. So the struggle is hard work done unwillingly.
  4. She did not need to convince her parents – they pushed her; she is “envious” of their claim, not of talent.

Answer: option (4) — had to work hard to perfect the art, though unwillingly

Trap“Envious” appears in the passage, but she envies the certainty others claim, not their talent.
Q138CUET 2025 · 13 May, Shift 1 · Q7NTA final key
Passage (summarised): born to dance (Q5–8)

Summary in our own words; the exam printed the full extract.

What role did her father play in her becoming a dancer?
  1. He gave his passive disapproval
  2. He was indifferent
  3. He was actively involved.
  4. He tried maintaining a harmonious atmosphere.
Concept to recallRead the exact line: “My father probably kept his peace to avoid argument.”
  1. “Kept his peace to avoid argument” = stayed quiet so there would be no conflict at home.
  2. That is keeping the atmosphere harmonious.
  3. No sign of disapproval; not “actively involved” (he was “silent”).

Answer: option (4) — He tried maintaining a harmonious atmosphere.

Trap“Silent father” tempts “indifferent”; but the passage gives his reason – to avoid argument – which is a purpose, not indifference.
Q139CUET 2025 · 13 May, Shift 1 · Q8NTA final key
Passage (summarised): born to dance (Q5–8)

Summary in our own words; the exam printed the full extract.

The seeds of the narrator's future vocation were sown when she ________.
  1. went willingly to the dance class
  2. pranced around the house imitating the dance steps from a movie
  3. was born with an innate ability to dance
  4. was encouraged by her father to take up dancing
Concept to recall“Seeds sown” = the first event that started it. Find the episode in the passage.
  1. At seven, after the Mumtaz Ali film, she pranced around the house imitating him.
  2. Watching that, her mother said “you are born to dance” – the start of her career.
  3. She never went willingly; the father was silent; the narrator doubts the “born to dance” idea.

Answer: option (2) — pranced around the house imitating the dance steps from a movie

TrapOption 3 repeats the mother’s words, which the narrator calls “dubious”.
Q140CUET 2024 · 15 May (pen & paper) · Code A · Q17NTA final key
Passage (summarised): growing up as Premchand’s granddaughter (Q17–22)

A memoir by a granddaughter of Premchand; the paper names no source.

When the narrator, in her late teens, could not decide which language to write in, her father told her that one’s mother tongue is the only true medium of creative expression. He, Sripat Rai, was a Hindi editor and critic who sometimes translated Hindi into English, and joked that a failed writer becomes a critic. His literary hopes came to rest on her; after reading the first story she sent from Melbourne he told her mother, “She will go far.”

She later wrote fiction in Hindi, and secretly felt something like shame at the idea of writing in English — it seemed wrong for Premchand’s granddaughter. The family had a “certain linguistic pride”.

Being his granddaughter followed her everywhere: a shopkeeper, the family cook, a tea vendor — almost everyone had been moved by something he wrote. This very “ubiquity”, and the reverence and love he inspired, made him too large for her to grasp when young. She even felt that, merely by being related to him and without reading him, she had “somehow inhaled his writing”. She actually read him much later.

The author grew up with the expectation that she would take up ______________ .
Fill in the blank with the correct option to complete the sentence.
  1. editorship of a magazine.
  2. translation of literary pieces.
  3. creative writing.
  4. the job of a critic.
Concept to recallReading comprehension: answer from what the passage says, not from general knowledge; reject options that over-state (always, only, completely) or reverse the text.
  1. The father’s literary hopes came to rest on her, he was glad she was inclined to writing, and her first story pleased him → creative writing.
  2. Editing, translating and criticism were the father’s work — and he joked that a failed writer becomes a critic.

Answer: option (3) — creative writing.

Q141CUET 2024 · 15 May (pen & paper) · Code A · Q18NTA final key
Passage (summarised): growing up as Premchand’s granddaughter (Q17–22)

A memoir by a granddaughter of Premchand; the paper names no source.

When the narrator, in her late teens, could not decide which language to write in, her father told her that one’s mother tongue is the only true medium of creative expression. He, Sripat Rai, was a Hindi editor and critic who sometimes translated Hindi into English, and joked that a failed writer becomes a critic. His literary hopes came to rest on her; after reading the first story she sent from Melbourne he told her mother, “She will go far.”

She later wrote fiction in Hindi, and secretly felt something like shame at the idea of writing in English — it seemed wrong for Premchand’s granddaughter. The family had a “certain linguistic pride”.

Being his granddaughter followed her everywhere: a shopkeeper, the family cook, a tea vendor — almost everyone had been moved by something he wrote. This very “ubiquity”, and the reverence and love he inspired, made him too large for her to grasp when young. She even felt that, merely by being related to him and without reading him, she had “somehow inhaled his writing”. She actually read him much later.

When her father said, “She will go far,” he meant that _______________ .
Fill in the blank with the correct option to complete the sentence.
  1. she will travel widely.
  2. she will achieve great heights in life.
  3. she will go too far, one of these days.
  4. she will settle in a far-off place.
Concept to recallIdiom: go far = be very successful. (Contrast go too far = exceed the limits of what is acceptable.)
  1. Said approvingly after reading her first story → she will be very successful.
  2. Options (1) and (4) read far literally; (3) is a different idiom with a negative sense.

Answer: option (2) — she will achieve great heights in life.

Q142CUET 2024 · 15 May (pen & paper) · Code A · Q19NTA final key
Passage (summarised): growing up as Premchand’s granddaughter (Q17–22)

Choose a Statement which is not true with respect to the passage :
  1. The author felt pressurized to write in Hindi because of her father.
  2. She felt obligated to carry on the legacy of Premchand.
  3. Her family was chauvinistic about the English language.
  4. She was in awe of the extensive reach of her grandfather’s writings.
Concept to recallReading comprehension: answer from what the passage says, not from general knowledge; reject options that over-state (always, only, completely) or reverse the text.
  1. The family’s “linguistic pride” was about Hindi; she felt shame at the thought of writing in English. So pride in English is the false statement.
  2. (1), (2), (4) are all supported: the father’s pronouncement stayed with her, it seemed wrong for Premchand’s granddaughter to write in English, and his ubiquity was “too large to comprehend”.

Answer: option (3) — Her family was chauvinistic about the English language.

Q143CUET 2024 · 15 May (pen & paper) · Code A · Q20NTA final key
Passage (summarised): growing up as Premchand’s granddaughter (Q17–22)

A memoir by a granddaughter of Premchand; the paper names no source.

When the narrator, in her late teens, could not decide which language to write in, her father told her that one’s mother tongue is the only true medium of creative expression. He, Sripat Rai, was a Hindi editor and critic who sometimes translated Hindi into English, and joked that a failed writer becomes a critic. His literary hopes came to rest on her; after reading the first story she sent from Melbourne he told her mother, “She will go far.”

She later wrote fiction in Hindi, and secretly felt something like shame at the idea of writing in English — it seemed wrong for Premchand’s granddaughter. The family had a “certain linguistic pride”.

Being his granddaughter followed her everywhere: a shopkeeper, the family cook, a tea vendor — almost everyone had been moved by something he wrote. This very “ubiquity”, and the reverence and love he inspired, made him too large for her to grasp when young. She even felt that, merely by being related to him and without reading him, she had “somehow inhaled his writing”. She actually read him much later.

Premchand became too large for her to understand mainly because of _____________ .
(A) his ability to connect with people from all walks of life.
(B) the fact that she feared him.
(C) the kind of love and reverence that he inspired in people.
(D) her constant anxiety of failing him.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
  1. (A) and (D) only.
  2. (A) and (C) only.
  3. (B) and (C) only.
  4. (C) and (D) only.
Concept to recallReading comprehension: answer from what the passage says, not from general knowledge; reject options that over-state (always, only, completely) or reverse the text.
  1. The passage says his ubiquity (readers from every walk of life — shopkeeper, cook, tea vendor) and the reverence and love he inspired made him too large to grasp → A and C.
  2. Fear (B) and anxiety of failing him (D) are never mentioned.

Answer: option (2) — (A) and (C) only.

‘Inhaled his writing’ refers to :
Choose the correct option from the following.
  1. imbibing his style subconsciously.
  2. being compelled to write like him.
  3. being influenced by what people said about him.
  4. her father’s expectation from her.
Concept to recallMetaphor: to inhale something is to take it in without effort or awareness.

Answer: option (1) — imbibing his style subconsciously.

Q146CUET 2024 · 29 May (Delhi re-scheduled) · Code A · Q45NTA final key
Passage (summarised): the Green Blazer (Q45–50)

From R. K. Narayan’s short story “The Green Blazer” (not named in the paper).

In a crowded, noisy bazaar — villagers in turbans, townsmen in coats, bare-bodied beggars, women in bright saris, people who “harangued”, haggled and greeted one another, a Bible-preacher booming and a health van’s loudspeaker “amplified on malaria” — a green blazer “stood out prominently” and seemed to “cry out an invitation”. Raju could not ignore it.

He kept half apart from the crowd, always afraid of being spotted by a policeman. Bare-bodied in a loin-cloth, with a huge turban hiding his face, he hoped to be “taken for” a village peasant. He sat on a pile of “cast-off banana stalks” and watched the crowd with concentration, for that was his profession: an idler by nature, he had just enough energy to put his hand into other people’s pockets. Each “venture” was a gamble; sometimes he gained nothing and was lucky to keep his fingers intact.

Why did the Green Blazer draw Raju's attention ?
  1. It was his favourite colour.
  2. It screamed to be followed.
  3. It merged well with the crowd.
  4. It was too conspicuous in that crowd.
Concept to recallReading comprehension: answer from what the passage says, not from general knowledge; reject options that over-state (always, only, completely) or reverse the text.
  1. The blazer “stood out prominently”; it could not be missed in the crowd → conspicuous.
  2. It also seemed to “cry out an invitation”, which is why NTA accepted (2) too.
  3. (3) is the opposite; (1) is not in the passage.

Answer: option (4) — It was too conspicuous in that crowd.

NoteNTA’s final key accepts both option (2) and option (4); either earned the marks.

Q150CUET 2024 · 19 Jul re-test · Shift 1 · Q1NTA final key
Passage (summarised): Kalam’s dream (Q1–6)

Source named in the paper: A P J Abdul Kalam, Ignited Minds.

On 30 September 2001 Kalam was flying from Ranchi to Bokaro when his helicopter crashed just before landing; everyone escaped unhurt. “Unfazed”, he went on with his programme in Bokaro. That night doctors suggested a “tranquilliser” to ease the shock, and he slept early but fitfully, full of contemplation.

In a vivid dream he stood in a moonlit desert with Mahatma Gandhi, Albert Einstein, Emperor Asoka, Abraham Lincoln and Caliph Omar. Asoka’s reflection on the Kalinga war stood for a shift from conquest to compassion and gave rise to Ahimsa Dharma. In this “profound” conversation the figures spoke of peace, equality and ethics, and Asoka stressed the futility of causing suffering.

On waking, Kalam reflected on the forces of good and destruction in the world, yet held firm to the belief that a lasting solution could be found. He decided to shift his focus from his scientific career, awards and teams to India’s children — nurturing enlightened individuals and meeting young minds.

What event prompted the author's contemplation in the passage?
  1. Meeting the revered figures
  2. The helicopter crash
  3. The scheduled programme in Bokaro
  4. Doctors' suggestions for a tranquilliser
Concept to recallReading comprehension: answer from what the passage says, not from general knowledge; reject options that over-state (always, only, completely) or reverse the text.
  1. The crash led to the shock, the tranquilliser and the disturbed sleep “filled with contemplation”.
  2. He met the figures only in the dream that followed; the programme and the tranquilliser were consequences.

Answer: option (2) — The helicopter crash

Q151CUET 2024 · 19 Jul re-test · Shift 1 · Q19NTA final key
Passage (summarised): Raghavan’s pebble (Q19–24)

A short story set in Malgudi; the paper names no source.

In the village of Malgudi, Raghavan collected colourful pebbles from the riverbank every morning; the villagers were puzzled at first but came to accept the habit as part of his character. One sunrise he found a pebble that shimmered with an “iridescent glow” and kept it in a small wooden box on his windowsill.

Rumours of the “enchanted pebble” drew visitors who believed it held the answers to life’s mysteries. The humble Raghavan shared his insights with them, stressing the beauty of simplicity and the magic of everyday moments.

His jealous neighbour Murrku plotted to steal the pebble and sell it, so that he could buy the most expensive doll for his daughter Rae’s birthday. He succeeded — but it made no difference: Rae’s birthday had already been made complete by a simple home-made toy Raghavan gave her. In chasing the costliest gift Murrku had forgotten her birthday, and he finally understood Raghavan’s simple philosophy.

Complete the sentence:
Raghavan's pebble was unique due to ___________.
  1. its size
  2. its iridescent glow
  3. its shape
  4. its weight
Concept to recallReading comprehension: answer from what the passage says, not from general knowledge; reject options that over-state (always, only, completely) or reverse the text.
  1. It “shimmered with an iridescent glow”, unlike any he had seen.
  2. Size, shape and weight are never mentioned.

Answer: option (2) — its iridescent glow

Source named in the paper: A P J Abdul Kalam, Ignited Minds.

On 30 September 2001 Kalam was flying from Ranchi to Bokaro when his helicopter crashed just before landing; everyone escaped unhurt. “Unfazed”, he went on with his programme in Bokaro. That night doctors suggested a “tranquilliser” to ease the shock, and he slept early but fitfully, full of contemplation.

In a vivid dream he stood in a moonlit desert with Mahatma Gandhi, Albert Einstein, Emperor Asoka, Abraham Lincoln and Caliph Omar. Asoka’s reflection on the Kalinga war stood for a shift from conquest to compassion and gave rise to Ahimsa Dharma. In this “profound” conversation the figures spoke of peace, equality and ethics, and Asoka stressed the futility of causing suffering.

On waking, Kalam reflected on the forces of good and destruction in the world, yet held firm to the belief that a lasting solution could be found. He decided to shift his focus from his scientific career, awards and teams to India’s children — nurturing enlightened individuals and meeting young minds.

What significant decision did Abdul Kalam make after awakening from the dream?
  1. Shift focus from scientific career to nurturing enlightened individuals.
  2. Continue with his scheduled programme despite the incident.
  3. Pursue more awards and accolades in his scientific field.
  4. Explore the moonlit desert with the historical figures from the dream.
Concept to recallReading comprehension: answer from what the passage says, not from general knowledge; reject options that over-state (always, only, completely) or reverse the text.
  1. He turned from his scientific career to India’s children and nurturing enlightened individuals.
  2. (2) happened before the dream; (3) is the reverse; (4) is the dream itself.

Answer: option (1) — Shift focus from scientific career to nurturing enlightened individuals.

NoteKey matched by Question ID 4641991508.
Q160CUET 2023 · 21 May, Shift 1 · Q1NTA final key
Passage (summarised): a boat on the river at dusk (Q1–5)

The paper names no source; the scene is the opening of Charles Dickens’s Our Mutual Friend.

A boat on the river carries two people: a powerful, weather-beaten man with untidy grey hair, and a dark-haired young woman of about twenty who looks so much like him that she is clearly his daughter. She rows easily; he holds the rudder-lines loosely and keeps an eager look-out.

He has no net, hook or line, so he is no fisherman; the boat has no cushion, no paint, no inscription, nothing but a rusty boat-hook and a coil of rope; it is too small to carry cargo. He is plainly looking for something, with an intent, searching gaze, watching every eddy of the falling tide and steering her by movements of his head. She watches his face, but her look holds “a touch of dread or horror”.

The boat is covered in slime and ooze and is in a “sodden state”, more like the river-bottom than the surface. The pair are clearly doing something they often do. He calls to her: “Keep her out, Lizzie. The tide runs strong here.”

What is the name of the girl sailing on the boat?
  1. Lucy
  2. Lizzie
  3. Laura
  4. Tracy
Concept to recallAnswer from what the passage states or clearly implies; reject options that add facts, exaggerate, or are merely silly.
  1. The last line is the father’s order to her: “Keep her out, Lizzie.”
  2. No other name occurs in the passage.

Answer: option (2) — Lizzie

Q165CUET 2023 · 7 Jun, Shift 1 · Q1NTA final key
Passage (summarised): poem “Love and a Question” (Q1–5)

The paper prints the title “Love and a Question” (a poem by Robert Frost), four stanzas of eight lines. Paraphrase, stanza by stanza:

Stanza I. At evening a stranger comes to the door and speaks politely to the bridegroom. He carries a green-white stick and has nothing with him but his care. He “asked with the eyes more than the lips” for shelter for the night, then turned and looked at the dark road ahead, with no lit window anywhere.

Stanza II. The bridegroom steps into the porch and suggests they both look at the sky and wonder what the night will bring. Woodbine leaves litter the yard, the berries are blue; it is autumn, and winter is already in the wind. He says he wishes he knew.

Stanza III. Inside, the bride sits alone in the dusk bending over the open fire, her face rosy in the glow, thinking of her heart’s desire. The bridegroom looks out at the “weary road” but sees only her within, and wishes he could keep her heart safe, locked in gold.

Stanza IV. He would gladly give the stranger bread, a purse, a heartfelt prayer (or a curse for the rich). What troubles him is whether it is right to let anyone spoil the love of two newly-weds by bringing sorrow into the bridal house. The poem ends with him still uncertain — “the bridegroom wished he knew”.

The mood of the poem is :
  1. Sombre and heavy
  2. Cheerful
  3. Celebratory
  4. Sad and dark
Concept to recallMood = the feeling the poem creates. Sombre = grave, serious, dark in tone; heavy = weighed down.
  1. A homeless stranger at nightfall, winter in the wind, and a bridegroom torn by a moral question: grave and serious.
  2. Cheerful and celebratory ignore the stranger and the dilemma (the wedding is only the setting).
  3. “Sad and dark” is tempting, but nothing tragic happens; the tone is thoughtful and grave rather than grief-stricken, so NTA’s answer is sombre and heavy.

Answer: option (1) — Sombre and heavy

NoteCollegedunia gives Sad and dark; NTA’s final key gives Sombre and heavy.
Q166CUET 2023 · 7 Jun, Shift 1 · Q11NTA final key
Passage (summarised): a tiger, two wolves and a safari jeep (Q11–15)

A first-person wildlife account; the paper names no source.

The narrator’s party hears the alarm call of a chital (spotted deer), which signals that a predator is near. Kuttapan and Gautam go to investigate while the others drive around to meet them. Moments later a loud roar stops the vehicle: a large three-year-old male tiger, who shares the territory with his brother, is strolling straight towards them, and walks casually past.

Their quiet “reverie” is broken by a commotion. Anil, the guide, whispers “Wolves!”: two Indian grey wolves stand rigid and alarmed in a clearing, yelping at the tiger. The tiger charges after them into the forest.

Again and again a wolf comes back to provoke him; the tiger glowers, his muscles twitch, and the wolf dashes away. Finally the tiger moves off and the wolf disappears. The narrator guesses the wolf was protecting cubs and wanted the tiger out of his territory. Left in peace, the tiger resumes his stroll.

Whose presence is announced in the beginning ?
  1. Chital
  2. Tiger
  3. Kuttapan
  4. Gautam
Concept to recallRead the sentence carefully: whose presence is the alarm call announcing?
  1. The chital’s alarm call is “announcing the presence of a predator” — the predator turns out to be the tiger.
  2. The chital is the one making the announcement, not the one whose presence is announced.

Answer: option (2) — Tiger

TrapChoosing Chital because it is the first animal named.
NoteCollegedunia gives Chital; NTA’s final key gives Tiger, which is what the sentence actually says.

  1. Inquisitive

Match List - I with List - II.
List-I (Aspects in poem)List-II (Stanzas)
(A) Contrast between the warm house and cold outside(I) Stanza II
(B) Ethical dilemma of the bridegroom(II) Stanza III
(C) Eerie atmosphere due to dark night and harsh weather(III) Stanza I

Q174CUET 2023 · 7 Jun, Shift 2 · Q6NTA final key
Passage (summarised): Charsky and the Italian improvisatore (after an epigraph from Derzhavin)

The extract opens with a short epigraph by the poet Derzhavin (on man as at once king and slave, worm and god).

Next day Charsky finds the Italian he met the day before in room 35 off a dark, dirty inn corridor. He announces success: a princess is offering the Italian her salon; at a large party the night before Charsky had won over “half Petersburg”. The Italian should print tickets and programmes — if not a triumph, there will at least be a profit.

The Italian is delighted, shows it in a spate of lively movements typical of a southerner, and says he knew Charsky would help: Charsky is a poet like himself, and “poets are splendid fellows”. To show his gratitude he offers to perform an improvisation on the spot.

Charsky asks whether he can manage without an audience, music or applause. The Italian dismisses the worry: a fellow poet is the best audience, whose quiet encouragement is worth more than storms of applause, and asks Charsky to sit and give him a theme.

__________ are splendid fellows.
  1. Poets
  2. Italians
  3. Boys
  4. Audience
Concept to recallFill-in-from-the-text questions: find the phrase and copy the subject exactly.
  1. The Italian says Charsky is a poet like himself and that “poets are splendid fellows”.

Answer: option (1) — Poets

Passage (summarised): Charsky and the Italian improvisatore (after an epigraph from Derzhavin)

The extract opens with a short epigraph by the poet Derzhavin (on man as at once king and slave, worm and god).

Next day Charsky finds the Italian he met the day before in room 35 off a dark, dirty inn corridor. He announces success: a princess is offering the Italian her salon; at a large party the night before Charsky had won over “half Petersburg”. The Italian should print tickets and programmes — if not a triumph, there will at least be a profit.

The Italian is delighted, shows it in a spate of lively movements typical of a southerner, and says he knew Charsky would help: Charsky is a poet like himself, and “poets are splendid fellows”. To show his gratitude he offers to perform an improvisation on the spot.

Charsky asks whether he can manage without an audience, music or applause. The Italian dismisses the worry: a fellow poet is the best audience, whose quiet encouragement is worth more than storms of applause, and asks Charsky to sit and give him a theme.

An improvisation is incomplete without __________.
  1. an audience
  2. music
  3. applause
  4. All the above
Concept to recallRead whose view the question reports: here it is Charsky’s question, which lists three things.
  1. Charsky asks whether the Italian can do without “an audience, without music, without the thunder of applause”.
  2. All three are named together, so (4).

Answer: option (4) — All the above

NoteThe Italian goes on to reject the idea, but the question paraphrases Charsky’s list.

He did it through __________.

Q178CUET 2023 · 10 Jun, Shift 2 · Q10NTA final key
Passage (summarised): Alphonse and Charles, one-time partners

Nobody knew where Alphonse got his money; the person most amazed by his dashing, luxurious way of life was his friend and former partner, Charles.

After the partnership was dissolved, most of the customers and the best connections drifted gradually to Charles — not because he worked against Alphonse, but simply because Charles was the more capable of the two. Working on his own, Alphonse, for all his promptness, charm and good looks, was plainly not fit to run an independent business.

One person did watch him closely: Charles followed every blunder, extravagance and loss “to a nicety” and wondered how Alphonse kept going. The two had practically grown up together — their mothers were cousins, the families lived in the same street in Paris, where nearness counts as much as kinship, and the boys went to the same school.

The passage is about:
  1. two friends
  2. two friends who turned rivals
  3. two enemies
  4. two strangers
Concept to recallTheme questions: pick the option that covers the whole arc, not just one part of it.
  1. They grew up together and were partners (friends).
  2. After the split they became competitors in business, Charles winning the custom and watching every failure of Alphonse.
  3. Friends who turned rivals.

Answer: option (2) — two friends who turned rivals

Trap‘two friends’ describes only the start; the passage is about how the relation changed.
Q179CUET 2023 · 10 Jun, Shift 2 · Q11NTA final key
Passage (summarised): a Keralite at the Poles

The writer, who grew up in warm, lush green Trivandrum full of sights, sounds and people, finds the Poles quiet. Winter brings an “eerie desolation” and near-silence; survival in the frigid, dark, windy land is only for the fittest, and one misstep can mean anything from an icy injury to a numbing death.

Life there is tenuous but humbling, physically, mentally and spiritually; nature shows its dual face — raw, brutal and unforgiving, yet nurturing and awe-inspiring.

As days shorten most life leaves for warmer lands; those who stay are surrounded by glacial beauty and an unearthly stillness. In midwinter the sun seems only a memory, but auroras of many colours shift and snake “like billowing curtains” across the black sky, a promise that light will return.

Even the emptiness deceives: look closely and a flock of penguins waddles out from behind an ice shelf on the Antarctic peninsula.

The writer indicates that only those who are fit can survive at the poles. For the others it can lead to:-
A. death
B. bitterness
C. icy-injury
D. loneliness
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. A Only
  2. B Only
  3. A and C Only
  4. B and D Only
Concept to recallDo not let an adjective in the text become an option on its own: ‘bitter’ describes death.
  1. A misstep can mean anything from an icy injury to a bitter, benumbed death → A and C.

Answer: option (3) — A and C Only

Trap‘bitter’ is an adjective for death, not ‘bitterness’ as a consequence.

A. he knew all to a nicety, and he wondered how Alphonse could keep going so long.

C. And there was one person who did observe him closely. Charles followed him step by step...

E. ...it arose simply from the fact that Charles was the more capable man of the two

  2. B-C-A-E-D
  3. D-B-E-C-A
  4. A-B-E-C-D

Q185CUET 2023 · 15 Jun, Shift 3 · Q11NTA final key
Passage (summarised): from the opening of Chris Cleave’s The Other Hand, with a blurb

The narrator, a young Nigerian woman, says that learning the Queen’s English is like scrubbing the “bright red varnish” off your toe nails on the morning after a dance: it is slow, and a stain of red always remains at the growing edges as a reminder of the good time. She learned it slowly but had plenty of time — two years locked in an immigration detention centre in Essex, in the south-east of the UK.

Why take the trouble? Older girls told her that to survive you must look good or talk even better: the plain and silent ones never seem to have their papers in order, and are repatriated — “sent home early”.

A blurb follows: The Other Hand is about a young woman who flees conflict in her village in the oil-rich region of southern Nigeria, enters the UK illegally and is held for a long time in a detention centre near London. Once freed, she searches for the two English people she knows — she met them years earlier, during a life-changing event on a beach in Nigeria; will they help her, and can she survive as an immigrant?

What is meant by ‘Queen’s English’ in the text given :
(A) Good, formal English
(B) Fluent, vernacular English
(C) English as spoken in the UK
(D) Good formal American English
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
  1. (A), (B) and (C) only
  2. (A), (B) and (D) only
  3. (A) and (B) only
  4. (A) and (C) only
Concept to recallThe Queen’s (King’s) English = standard, correct British English.
  1. It is correct, formal English (A) as spoken in Britain (C).
  2. ‘Vernacular’ means everyday local speech, and American English is the wrong variety.

Answer: option (4) — (A) and (C) only

What does the author suggest, would have happened if she hadn’t learnt the Queen’s English ?
  1. She would have survived in England.
  2. She would have been repatriated.
  3. She would have stayed longer is detention.
  4. She couldn’t have gone back home easily.

Q189CUET 2023 · 18 Jun, Shift 1 · Q1NTA final key
Passage (summarised): the unhappy literary life (Q1–5)

The writer argues that a literary life is mostly an unhappy one: a genius must pay “the penalty of genius”, and a merely talented writer faces endless cares. Beyond the pain of composing and the artist’s frustration at never fully expressing himself, there is the constant struggle to reach the public.

Young writers believe they need only print a book to be hailed instantly as a new light in literature. They will not accept that editors and publishers are practical businessmen, “mere brokers” working on profit and loss, in no hurry to put good literature before readers. Once a book is out, the writer must “run the gauntlet of the critics”, who seem to a beginner like enemies thirsting for his scalp. An older author learns to treat criticism as clowning, but sensitive souls may give up writing altogether — Keats is offered as a fine spirit hounded to death by savage reviews. The passage ends by saying an author should never publicly defend himself: silence is the only safeguard and the only dignified protest.

Why is the literary life mostly an unhappy one?
  1. Most people don't understand literary people
  2. They have to suffer the penalty of genius
  3. Literary life is not about richness
  4. They do not get the publishers easily
Concept to recallAnswer from what the passage states; reject options that are true in general but not said there.
  1. The opening sentence gives the reason directly: a writer of genius must suffer “the penalty of genius”.
  2. Publishers and critics are mentioned later as further troubles, not as the reason given for the unhappiness, so (4) is only part of the picture.
  3. Nothing is said about people failing to understand writers or about wealth.

Answer: option (2) — They have to suffer the penalty of genius

Q193CUET 2023 · 18 Jun, Shift 3 · Q1NTA final key
Poem extract (paraphrased): “No Man is an Island” (Q1–5)

The extract, printed under the title “No Man is an Island”, is the well-known passage from John Donne’s Devotions upon Emergent Occasions (Meditation XVII, 1624).

Paraphrase. No human being is complete in himself like an island; each is a piece of a larger continent, part of the mainland. If the sea washes away even one small lump of earth (a “clod”), Europe is made smaller — just as it would be if a whole headland, or the estate of a friend or of one’s own, were lost. In the same way, the death of any person diminishes the speaker, because he is bound up with all mankind. So one should never send to ask whose death the funeral bell is ringing for: “It tolls for thee”.

Form. Several successive lines begin with the same words (“As well as if …”, “No man … / Every man …”), and the whole piece is an extended metaphor of land and sea for human connectedness.

What is the essential idea of the passage?
  1. The passage signifies a connection between all of humankind.
  2. The passage signifies that all aquatic animals are connected.
  3. The poet is uninvolved in mankind.
  4. The poet wants to live in an island.
Concept to recallThe central idea is the claim the whole piece builds to, not a literal reading of its images.
  1. Every image (island, continent, clod, bell) makes one point: each person is part of mankind, so every death touches us all.
  2. (3) contradicts “I am involved in mankind”; (2) and (4) read the sea imagery literally.

Answer: option (1) — The passage signifies a connection between all of humankind.

Q194CUET 2023 · 18 Jun, Shift 3 · Q10NTA final key
Passage (summarised): a folk tale of Satto and the mahua flowers (Q6–10)

An “age-old tale”, given in translation. A mother and her daughter Satto lived in a village when the forests were full of fruit and flowers. The village women and girls gathered the sweet flowers of the mahua tree, stored them at home and ate them later.

One day they all brought flowers home without drying them. While her mother was out, Satto dried theirs, and the flowers shrank. Coming home to find only a few, the mother assumed Satto had eaten them or given them away to the other girls, and in a blind rage beat her to death. The village women told her she had killed her daughter over a trifle and asked her to soak the flowers in water; when she did, they swelled up until the whole room was full of them. Overcome with remorse, the mother died of grief and was reborn as the pandak bird, which still sings that the mahuas were in proper quantity.

What happened Satto's mother soaked the flowers in water?
  1. The entire room was filled with flowers as they soaked up
  2. Satto came back to life
  3. The flowers dissolved in water
  4. The entire room was full of water
Concept to recallAnswer from what the passage states; reject options that are true in general but not said there.
  1. Soaked, the flowers swelled until the whole room was filled with them — proving none were missing.

Answer: option (1) — The entire room was filled with flowers as they soaked up

Q195CUET 2023 · 18 Jun, Shift 3 · Q12NTA final key
Passage (summarised): the archaeologist and Malgudi (Q11–16)

The narrator recalls working as assistant to a famous archaeologist, roaming the country digging for antiquities — enjoyable work, though cynics mockingly called them “grave-diggers”. The master was a timeless, unworldly man who wanted neither food nor shelter nor riches so long as he could gaze undisturbed at an old coin or a chip of a burial urn.

He had dug up almost every part of India and uncovered valuable knowledge of remote centuries; his monographs on his excavations filled shelves in all the important libraries. Then he was suddenly inspired with the idea that Malgudi district was well worth digging. Hearing that he was staying in the dak bungalow and needed an assistant, the narrator went to him within the hour and found him on the floor amid pots, beads, old coins and palm leaves, examining them with a lens and taking notes.

LIST ILIST II
A. The archaeologist had keen interest inI. all the important libraries
B. The archaeologist was in need ofII. almost all parts of India
C. His monographs on excavations filled inIII. old coin or chip of a burial urn
D. The archaeologist had worked inIV. an assistant
  1. A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I
  2. A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II
  3. A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I
  4. A-I, B-III, C-II, D-IV
Concept to recallAnswer from what the passage states; reject options that are true in general but not said there.
  1. Keen interest → an old coin or chip of a burial urn (III); in need of → an assistant (IV);
  2. monographs filled → all the important libraries (I); worked in → almost all parts of India (II).

Answer: option (2) — A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

Q199CUET 2023 · 18 Jun, Shift 3 · Q4NTA final key
Poem extract (paraphrased): “No Man is an Island” (Q1–5)

The extract, printed under the title “No Man is an Island”, is the well-known passage from John Donne’s Devotions upon Emergent Occasions (Meditation XVII, 1624).

Paraphrase. No human being is complete in himself like an island; each is a piece of a larger continent, part of the mainland. If the sea washes away even one small lump of earth (a “clod”), Europe is made smaller — just as it would be if a whole headland, or the estate of a friend or of one’s own, were lost. In the same way, the death of any person diminishes the speaker, because he is bound up with all mankind. So one should never send to ask whose death the funeral bell is ringing for: “It tolls for thee”.

Form. Several successive lines begin with the same words (“As well as if …”, “No man … / Every man …”), and the whole piece is an extended metaphor of land and sea for human connectedness.

What does the clause "for whom the bell tolls" entail?
  1. The arrival of a guest
  2. The arrival of death
  3. The Sunday church mass
  4. Time to Pray
Concept to recallA church bell tolled slowly announced a death or funeral.
  1. The poem is about every man’s death diminishing us; the bell is the funeral bell.
  2. So asking for whom it tolls is asking who has died → the arrival of death.

Answer: option (2) — The arrival of death

Trap“Church mass” and “time to pray” are what bells ring for; toll is the slow ringing for the dead.
Q200CUET 2023 · 18 Jun, Shift 3 · Q5NTA final key
Poem extract (paraphrased): “No Man is an Island” (Q1–5)

The extract, printed under the title “No Man is an Island”, is the well-known passage from John Donne’s Devotions upon Emergent Occasions (Meditation XVII, 1624).

Paraphrase. No human being is complete in himself like an island; each is a piece of a larger continent, part of the mainland. If the sea washes away even one small lump of earth (a “clod”), Europe is made smaller — just as it would be if a whole headland, or the estate of a friend or of one’s own, were lost. In the same way, the death of any person diminishes the speaker, because he is bound up with all mankind. So one should never send to ask whose death the funeral bell is ringing for: “It tolls for thee”.

Form. Several successive lines begin with the same words (“As well as if …”, “No man … / Every man …”), and the whole piece is an extended metaphor of land and sea for human connectedness.

'No man is an Island' signifies that-
  1. No man stands in isolation
  2. All of humanity is connected
  3. No man exists as a landmass
  4. No island is inhabited by men
Concept to recallAn island is cut off on all sides; denying that a man is one means no one is isolated.
  1. The line itself says a person is not an isolated unit → no man stands in isolation.
  2. (2) is the poem’s wider conclusion, which the next lines draw; NTA keys the literal sense of the phrase.
  3. (3) and (4) read the metaphor literally.

Answer: option (1) — No man stands in isolation

NoteOptions (1) and (2) are two ways of saying the same thing; NTA’s final key gives (1).

Q204CUET 2023 · 19 Jun, Shift 2 · Q1NTA final key
Passage (summarised): “not an ordinary ten-year-old” (Q1–5)

A ten-year-old boy narrates. He does ordinary things — eats ice cream, rides his bike, plays ball, owns an Xbox — and these make him feel ordinary inside. But ordinary children do not make other children run away screaming in playgrounds, and they are not stared at wherever they go.

Given one wish from a magic lamp, he would ask for a normal face that nobody noticed, so that he could walk down a street without people seeing him and then quickly looking away. He thinks he is not ordinary only because no one else sees him that way; by now he is used to his looks and knows how to pretend.

He and his parents have learnt not to notice the faces people make. His sister Via is the exception: she gets angry at rudeness. Once, when older children made noises at him in a playground, he himself did not hear them, but Via did and started yelling at them. He says he is not like that.

What makes the 10-year-old narrator ordinary ?
(A) He rides his bike
(B) He plays ball
(C) He makes children run away
(D) He gets stared at
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
  1. (A) only
  2. (C) only
  3. (A) and (B)
  4. (C) and (D)
Concept to recallAnswer from what the passage states; reject options that are true in general but not said there.
  1. Riding his bike and playing ball are among the “ordinary things” he lists.
  2. Making children run away and being stared at are what make him not ordinary.

Answer: option (3) — (A) and (B)

Trap(C) and (D) are the opposite list — what sets him apart.

Q208CUET 2023 · 19 Jun, Shift 2 · Q6NTA final key
Passage (summarised): a young mother alone at night (Q6–10)

A very young woman, alone in a hut with a galvanised-iron roof, eats a little, drinks some milk, and without lighting a fire or a candle creeps into bed with her baby.

She wakes, surprised that she had slept at all, with her heart beating wildly. Lying still, she puts her arms round the baby and silently begs it not to wake. In the moonlight on the front of the house she sees one of the cracks in the wall darken with a shadow. She hears the dog growl, the man outside turn hastily, the thud of a blow on the dog’s ribs, and the dog howl and run off. The shadow then moves from crack to crack as the man tries every spot from which he might see in. She thinks of ways to make him believe she is not alone, but speaking would wake the baby, which she dreads as if it were the only danger, so she keeps praying that the baby will not wake or cry.

The girl sees a shadow against which of the following sources of light ?
  1. fire
  2. candlelight
  3. a well lit roof
  4. moonlight
Concept to recallAnswer from what the passage states; reject options that are true in general but not said there.
  1. She lit no fire and no candle; the moon shone on the front of the house and a crack darkened with a shadow.

Answer: option (4) — moonlight

TrapFire and candle are named in the passage only to say she did not light them.

Q212CUET 2023 · 21 Jun, Shift 1 · Q1NTA final key
Passage (summarised): a Brahman in search of the Ganges (F. W. Bain)

An old Brahman, carrying his pot and staff, is doing penance “for the expiation of sin” on the banks of what he believes is the Ganges. A passing Pashupata ascetic laughs at him: this miserable puddle has nothing to do with the Ganges, which is hundreds of miles away and dwarfs this brook as Mount Meru dwarfs an ant-hill. Thanking him, the Brahman travels on to a broad river, rejoices, and bathes in it daily for five years — until a Kapalika tells him he is wasting his time on a river of no sanctity: is a jackal a lion, or a Chandala a Brahman? Sighing, the Brahman again takes up pot and staff.

Now old and weakened by penance, he toils on through the heat; the sun beats on his head “like the thunderbolt of Indra” and gives him fever. At last he collapses, drags himself up a low hill, and sees the mighty Ganges below, crowded with pilgrims. Crying out to Mother Ganges that he has pursued her all his life only to die helpless in sight of her, he dies of a broken heart without reaching its shore.

(The file as mirrored begins the passage at the ascetic’s arrival; any earlier opening is not shown.)

What was the name of the ascetic who was talking to the Brahman ?
  1. Brahmdatta
  2. Pashupata
  3. Saumyadatta
  4. Pushpata
Concept to recallPick the name the passage itself gives: ‘a Pashupata ascetic’.
  1. The ascetic who mocks the ‘puddle’ is the Pashupata (a Shaiva order).
  2. ‘Pushpata’ is a look-alike spelling; the other two names do not appear.

Answer: option (2) — Pashupata

TrapPushpata vs Pashupata — read the spelling.

Passage (summarised): a Brahman in search of the Ganges (F. W. Bain)

An old Brahman, carrying his pot and staff, is doing penance “for the expiation of sin” on the banks of what he believes is the Ganges. A passing Pashupata ascetic laughs at him: this miserable puddle has nothing to do with the Ganges, which is hundreds of miles away and dwarfs this brook as Mount Meru dwarfs an ant-hill. Thanking him, the Brahman travels on to a broad river, rejoices, and bathes in it daily for five years — until a Kapalika tells him he is wasting his time on a river of no sanctity: is a jackal a lion, or a Chandala a Brahman? Sighing, the Brahman again takes up pot and staff.

Now old and weakened by penance, he toils on through the heat; the sun beats on his head “like the thunderbolt of Indra” and gives him fever. At last he collapses, drags himself up a low hill, and sees the mighty Ganges below, crowded with pilgrims. Crying out to Mother Ganges that he has pursued her all his life only to die helpless in sight of her, he dies of a broken heart without reaching its shore.

(The file as mirrored begins the passage at the ascetic’s arrival; any earlier opening is not shown.)

Who said, “I am performing penance, for the expiation of sin ....”
  1. The Brahman
  2. Pashupata ascetic
  3. The Kapalika
  4. Brahmadatta
Concept to recallTrack speakers in dialogue: the ascetic asks, the Brahman replies.
  1. The ascetic asks ‘what are you doing here?’ and ‘he replied’ — the Brahman, who is doing penance.

Answer: option (1) — The Brahman

Q216CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 2 · Q1NTA final key
Passage (summarised): poem ‘A River’ (A. K. Ramanujan)

The poem opens in Madurai, “city of temples and poets”, whose poets sang of cities and temples. Every summer the river there shrinks to a trickle, exposing ribs of sand; straw and women’s hair choke the water-gates at the rusty bars of bridges that are “patches of repair all over”. The wet stones shine like sleepy crocodiles and the dry ones look like shaven water-buffaloes lounging in the sun.

The second stanza says the (old) poet sang only of the floods: “He was there for a day” when the floods came. People talked of the rising inches, the exact number of cobbled steps the water covered on the bathing places, and how it carried off three village houses, one pregnant woman and a couple of cows named Gopi and Brinda, “as usual”.

What do the ‘wet stones’ and ‘dry stones’ in the poem compared to ?
  1. Cobbled steps and concrete steps
  2. Water buffaloes and Crocodiles
  3. Cows named Gopi and Brinda
  4. Crocodiles and water buffaloes
Concept to recallA simile pairs each thing with its image in order: wet stones → sleepy crocodiles; dry ones → shaven water-buffaloes.
  1. Wet stones glisten “like sleepy crocodiles”; the dry ones are “shaven water-buffaloes”.
  2. So the pair, in the order asked (wet, dry), is crocodiles and water buffaloes.
  3. Option (2) names the same animals in the wrong order; (1) and (3) are other details of the poem.

Answer: option (4) — Crocodiles and water buffaloes

TrapOrder matters: (2) reverses the pairing.
Q217CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 2 · Q11NTA final key
Passage (summarised): from The God of Small Things (Arundhati Roy), ch. 1

It is raining when Rahel returns to Ayemenem; the rain falls in “slanting silver ropes” that plough up the loose earth. The old house on the hill wears its steep, gabled roof like a low hat; its mossy walls are soft and bulging with damp. The overgrown garden is full of the whisper and scurry of small lives: a rat snake rubs itself on a glistening stone, bullfrogs cruise the scummy pond, a drenched mongoose crosses the driveway.

The house looks empty — doors and windows locked, verandah bare — but the sky-blue Plymouth is still parked outside, and inside Baby Kochamma (Navomi Ipe, Rahel’s grandfather’s younger sister, her baby grand-aunt) is still alive. Rahel has not come to see her, though; she has come to see her brother Estha. They are two-egg (“dizygotic”) twins, Estha the elder by eighteen minutes. They never looked alike, so relatives and the Syrian Orthodox bishops who visited the Ayemenem House for donations never asked “which is which?”; the confusion lay somewhere deeper.

Why had Rahel come to see ?
  1. Bishops
  2. Her sister
  3. Baby Kochamma
  4. Estha
Concept to recallRead the sentence that states purpose directly: Rahel ‘had come to see her brother, Estha’.
  1. The passage first says Rahel had not come to see Baby Kochamma.
  2. It then says she came to see her brother Estha.
  3. The bishops are past visitors; Rahel has no sister in the passage.

Answer: option (4) — Estha

TrapBaby Kochamma is mentioned just before — and explicitly ruled out.

Passage (summarised): from The God of Small Things (Arundhati Roy), ch. 1

How are Estha and Rahel related ?
(A) They are unidentical twins
(B) They are dizygotic twins
(C) They are identical twins
(D) They are two egg twins
(E) They are twin sisters
Choose the correct answer :
  1. (A), (B) and (D) only
  2. (B) only
  3. (C) and (E) only
  4. (C) and (D) only
Concept to recallDizygotic = from two eggs = fraternal (non-identical) twins.
  1. The passage: ‘two-egg twins’, called ‘dizygotic’ by doctors — (B) and (D).
  2. Two-egg twins are not identical, so (A) also holds, and (C) is false.
  3. Estha is Rahel’s brother, so (E) twin sisters is false.

Answer: option (1) — (A), (B) and (D) only

Trap(2) ‘(B) only’ misses that (A) and (D) say the same thing in other words.

  1. Kochamma

Passage (summarised): poem ‘A River’ (A. K. Ramanujan)

The poem opens in Madurai, “city of temples and poets”, whose poets sang of cities and temples. Who is ‘He’ in the second stanza ?
  1. The poet
  2. Gopi
  3. Brinda
  4. A person from the village
Concept to recallA pronoun refers to the nearest suitable noun: here ‘The poet only sang of the floods / He was there for a day’.

How is the drainage system in the city ?
  1. there is no drainage system in the city

  3. freshly repaired

Q223CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 2 · Q5NTA final key
Passage (summarised): poem ‘A River’ (A. K. Ramanujan)

The poem opens in Madurai, “city of temples and poets”, whose poets sang of cities and temples. Every summer the river there shrinks to a trickle, exposing ribs of sand; straw and women’s hair choke the water-gates at the rusty bars of bridges that are “patches of repair all over”. The wet stones shine like sleepy crocodiles and the dry ones look like shaven water-buffaloes lounging in the sun.

The second stanza says the (old) poet sang only of the floods: “He was there for a day” when the floods came. People talked of the rising inches, the exact number of cobbled steps the water covered on the bathing places, and how it carried off three village houses, one pregnant woman and a couple of cows named Gopi and Brinda, “as usual”.

How did other poet sing about Madurai ?
(A) other poets sang of cities and temples
(B) other poets sang only of the flood
(C) other poets sang of the drought
(D) other poets sang of animals
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (C) only
  2. (A) only
  3. (A) and (B) only
  4. (C) and (D) only
Concept to recallLocate each claim in the text; the poets of Madurai ‘sang of cities and temples’, and ‘the poet only sang of the floods’.
  1. (A) is stated in the opening lines.
  2. (B): the poets sang only of the floods, never of the dry summer river — NTA accepts it.
  3. No poet sings of the drought (C) or of animals (D); the drought is the speaker’s own description.

Answer: option (3) — (A) and (B) only

Trap(2) ‘(A) only’ misses the poem’s central irony that the poets sang only of floods.
Q224CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q1NTA final key
Passage (summarised): a stranger arrives at a hill village

The narrator sits on a rock beside a hut on the south edge of a ridge about fifty yards wide; the village lies on the north face of the hill, so it cannot be seen from the hut. After ten minutes a head appears over the crest from the village side, then a second and a third: his friend the water-carrier has wasted no time telling the village he has arrived.

He explains a custom: when strangers in India meet to get information from each other, they avoid raising (‘broaching’) the real subject until the very end, and fill the time by asking about each other’s private affairs — marriage, children, job, pay. Questions that elsewhere would “earn one a thick ear” are asked so artlessly in these hills that nobody who has lived among the people dreams of taking offence.

Where was the narrator sitting when he saw someone coming ?
  1. the rock
  2. the crest
  3. the ridge
  4. the hill
Concept to recallLocate the detail: the narrator had been on the rock for ‘ten minutes’ when a head appeared.
  1. He was sitting on the rock.
  2. The crest is where the heads appeared; ridge and hill are the wider setting.

Answer: option (1) — the rock

Trap‘the crest’ is where the newcomers were, not the narrator.
Q225CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q13NTA final key
Passage (summarised): blackberry picking with grandparents

As a child of seven or eight, the narrator went blackberry picking with his grandparents in late August, when the berries were ripe. Grandad drove them in his old van — uncomfortable and not very safe, but it had a character no sleek new car could match, and the boy enjoyed bouncing along.

They always went to the same spot, where wild bushes lined the road as far as the eye could see; the road overlooked a small pitch-and-putt course where golfers “ambled sedately” from hole to hole.

They picked for hours. Nana warned him not to eat any berries before washing them but turned a blind eye as he gorged; he liked the bitter unripe red ones, but the green ones were too much even for him. By evening Grandad hauled a half-full bin bag back to the van, juice dripping; Nana would later make apple and blackberry tarts and jam. The boy’s stomach hurt, his hands stung from thorn pricks and were stained dark purple — and he always enjoyed those days.

From the following list of events and activities in the passage, choose the incorrect one :
  1. They would pick blueberries for several hours.
  2. The juice from the blueberries would bleed onto the ground.
  3. It was usually late August when the blueberries fully ripened.
  4. Grandma would drive the narrator in her old van.
Concept to recallCheck who did what: it was Grandad who drove the old van.
  1. Picking for hours, juice bleeding onto the ground and late-August ripening are all in the passage.
  2. The van belonged to and was driven by Grandad, not Grandma, so (4) is incorrect.

Answer: option (4) — Grandma would drive the narrator in her old van.

NoteAll four options say ‘blueberries’ where the passage has blackberries; NTA’s key treats that as a slip and marks only the driver error.

What would happen to the narrator’s hands at the end of the day ?
  1. It would amble sedately.
  2. It was swollen and stained purplish red.
  3. It stung from constant thorn pricks.
  4. It was broken as he fell from a blueberry tree.

  1. The passage says his hands stung from thorn pricks — (3).
  2. (2) adds ‘swollen’ and changes the colour; (1) is about golfers; (4) never happens.
