Trap(1) treats the sentence as positive.
Q863CUET 2023 · 21 Jun, Shift 1 · Q47NTA final key
Choose the correct sentence :
(A) He said that honesty has been the best policy.
(B) He said that honesty had been the best policy.
(C) He said that honesty was the best policy.
(D) He said that honesty is the best policy.
(E) He said that honesty will be the best policy.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (A) and (B) only
  2. (C) and (B) only
  3. (A), (B) and (C) only
  4. (D) only
Concept to recallA universal truth keeps the present tense in reported speech even after a past reporting verb.
  1. ‘Honesty is the best policy’ is a proverb/universal truth → no back-shift.
  2. So only (D).

Answer: option (4) — (D) only

Q864CUET 2023 · 21 Jun, Shift 1 · Q50NTA final key
Identify the adjective clause in the following sentence :
The reason why I did this is obvious.
  1. why I did this
  2. reason why I
  3. this is obvious
  4. the reason why I did
Concept to recall‘the reason why …’: the why-clause qualifies the noun reason, so it is an adjective (relative) clause.
  1. Clause = subject + verb with its connective: ‘why I did this’.
  2. It describes reason → adjective clause.

Answer: option (1) — why I did this

Q865CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 2 · Q16NTA final key
Choose the most appropriate option which best expresses the same sentence in Passive/Active Voice
Honey is made by bees.
  1. Bees made honey
  2. Bees are making honey
  3. Bees make honey
  4. Bees makes honey
Concept to recallVoice change keeps the tense: simple-present passive is made ↔ simple-present active make; verb agrees with the new subject.
  1. ‘is made’ = simple present passive.
  2. Active: subject bees (plural) + make + object honey.
  3. (1) is past, (2) continuous, (4) breaks agreement (bees makes).

Answer: option (3) — Bees make honey

Q866CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 2 · Q17NTA final key
Choose the most appropriate option which best expresses the same sentence in Passive/Active Voice ?
The news surprised us.
  1. We are surprised at the news.
  2. We were surprised by the news
  3. We are surprised by the news
  4. We were surprised at the news
Concept to recallSimple past active → was/were + V3 + by agent.
  1. ‘surprised’ is simple past, so the passive needs were surprised.
  2. The agent of a passive is introduced by by: ‘by the news’.
  3. (1), (3) shift to present; (4) uses at, an adjectival idiom rather than the strict passive.

Answer: option (2) — We were surprised by the news

Trap‘surprised at’ is idiomatic English, but a voice-change answer keeps by.
Q867CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 2 · Q18NTA final key
Choose the most appropriate option which best expresses the same sentence in Indirect/Direct speech.
She asked me if I was going to college.
  1. She asked me, “Will you go to college ?”
  2. She said to me “Are you going to college ?”
  3. She asked to me, “Was I going to college ?”
  4. She said, “Am I going to college ?”
Concept to recallIndirect → direct: asked if becomes said to …, “question?”; past continuous back-shifts to present continuous; I (listener) → you.
  1. ‘was going’ in reported speech ⇒ ‘are going’ in the direct words.
  2. The listener (me/I) is addressed as you: “Are you going to college?”
  3. (1) changes the tense to future; (3) and (4) keep the reported pronoun I, and (3) has the ungrammatical ‘asked to me’.

Answer: option (2) — She said to me “Are you going to college ?”

Q868CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 2 · Q19NTA final key
Choose the most appropriate option which best expresses the same sentence in Indirect/Direct speech.
He said, “Sita, when is the next train ?”
  1. He said to Sita when the next train was.
  2. He asked Sita when the next train was.
  3. He asked Sita about the next train.
  4. He asked when the next train is.
Concept to recallWh-question in reported speech: asked + wh-word + subject + verb (statement order), tense back-shifted (is → was).
  1. Reporting verb for a question: asked (not said to); the vocative Sita becomes the object.
  2. Question order becomes statement order and is → was: ‘when the next train was’.
  3. (3) loses the content; (4) drops Sita and keeps is.

Answer: option (2) — He asked Sita when the next train was.

Q869CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 2 · Q28NTA final key
Convert the following sentence from Assertive to Exclamatory :
I wish I could meet my friend again.
  1. If only could meet my friend again!
  2. My friend I would like meet very much.
  3. A meeting with my friend is what I wish.
  4. I have one wish! I want meet my friend again!
Concept to recall‘I wish …’ becomes the exclamatory ‘If only …!’ (or ‘Would that …!’).
  1. ‘If only I could meet my friend again!’ is the standard form; option (1) is that (as printed, missing ‘I’).
  2. (2) and (3) are assertive; (4) is ungrammatical (‘want meet’).

Answer: option (1) — If only could meet my friend again!

Q870CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 2 · Q29NTA final key
Convert the following sentence from Assertive to Exclamatory :
The evening is very beautiful.
  1. An evening it is and that too a beautiful one.
  2. Beautiful is this evening!
  3. How beautiful is the evening!
  4. What beauty is that evening!
Concept to recall‘very + adjective’ → ‘How + adjective + …!’
  1. Replace very beautiful with How beautiful and add an exclamation mark.
  2. (2) inverts but changes the to this; (4) changes the adjective to a noun and the to that.

Answer: option (3) — How beautiful is the evening!

Q871CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 2 · Q34NTA final key
Which of the following elements comes last in a business letter ?
  1. Date
  2. Signature
  3. Body of the letter
  4. Courteous leave taking
Concept to recallBusiness-letter order: sender’s address → date → inside address → salutation → subject → body → complimentary close (leave-taking) → signature.
  1. The courteous leave-taking (‘Yours faithfully’) precedes the signature.
  2. Date and body come earlier. So the signature is last.

Answer: option (2) — Signature

Q872CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 2 · Q35NTA final key
Which of the following is not an appropriate subscription for a business letter ?
  1. Yours Sincerely
  2. Yours faithfully
  3. Warm Regards
  4. Yours Lovingly
Concept to recallSubscription (complimentary close) must match the letter’s formality; ‘Yours lovingly’ is for family.
  1. ‘Yours faithfully/sincerely’ are formal; ‘Warm regards’ is acceptable semi-formal business usage.
  2. ‘Yours lovingly’ belongs only in personal letters.

Answer: option (4) — Yours Lovingly

Q873CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 2 · Q44NTA final key
Identify the kind of adverbs in the following sentence :
Things are no better at present.
  1. Adverbs of degree or Quality
  2. Adverb of Time
  3. Adverb of Frequency
  4. Adverb of Place
Concept to recallAdverbs of degree answer ‘how much / to what extent?’: very, too, much, no (better), any (better), quite.
  1. ‘no’ in ‘no better’ modifies the comparative better and tells to what extent → adverb of degree.
  2. ‘at present’ is an adverbial phrase of time, but it is a phrase, not the adverb the question targets — NTA keys degree.

Answer: option (1) — Adverbs of degree or Quality

Trap‘at present’ pulls towards Time; the single-word adverb is no.
Q874CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 2 · Q45NTA final key
Fill in the blank in the following sentence with an adverbs of manner :
She sings __________.
  1. everyday
  2. delightfully
  3. a song
  4. far better than him
Concept to recallAdverb of manner answers ‘how?’, usually an -ly word.
  1. How does she sing? ‘delightfully’.
  2. ‘everyday’ is time/frequency; ‘a song’ is an object; (4) is a comparison (and should be ‘than he’).

Answer: option (2) — delightfully

Q875CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 2 · Q46NTA final key
Fill in the blank in the following sentence with the most appropriate question Tag :
Have some more rice, ________ ?
  1. wouldn’t you
  2. can you
  3. did you
  4. will you
Concept to recallAn imperative (request/offer) takes the tag will you? (or won’t you?).
  1. ‘Have some more rice’ is an imperative offer.
  2. Imperatives take ‘will you’.

Answer: option (4) — will you

Q876CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 2 · Q50NTA final key
Fill in the blanks with suitable Adjective clause.
Choose the appropriate option.
The doctor has given me medicines _________.
  1. Which I must take
  2. Where I must take
  3. When I must take
  4. What I must take
Concept to recallAn adjective (relative) clause describing a thing begins with which/that; where qualifies places, when times.
  1. The clause qualifies medicines (things) → which.
  2. What cannot follow a noun antecedent.

Answer: option (1) — Which I must take

Q877CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q16NTA final key
Change the following sentences into active voice and choose the correct option :
The shipment will be sent by Friday.
  1. By Friday the shipment will be sent by us.
  2. We will send the shipment by Friday.
  3. We will have sent the shipment by Friday.
  4. By Friday the shipment will have been sent.
Concept to recallSimple future passive will be sent ↔ simple future active will send; supply an agent (we).
  1. ‘by Friday’ is a time phrase, not the agent; the agent is unstated, so use we.
  2. Active: ‘We will send the shipment by Friday.’
  3. (1) and (4) are still passive; (3) changes the tense to future perfect.

Answer: option (2) — We will send the shipment by Friday.

Q878CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q17NTA final key
Identify the sentence written in passive voice :
  1. someone stole my watch
  2. we expected him to call
  3. you are requested to complete the project
  4. you must deliver this passage
Concept to recallPassive = form of be + past participle, the subject receiving the action.
  1. ‘are requested’ = be + V3: the subject you receives the request.
  2. The others have doers as subjects (someone stole, we expected, you must deliver).

Answer: option (3) — you are requested to complete the project

Q879CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q18NTA final key
Choose the correct form of reported verb when the following sentence is changed to indirect speech :
She says, “I enjoy walking”.
  1. I enjoy
  2. I enjoyed
  3. She enjoys
  4. She enjoyed
Concept to recallReporting verb in the present (says) ⇒ no back-shift of tense; only the pronoun changes.
  1. says is present, so enjoy stays present.
  2. I becomes she, and the verb agrees: she enjoys.

Answer: option (3) — She enjoys

Trap(4) back-shifts as if the reporting verb were said.
Q880CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q19NTA final key
Choose the correct form of reported speech from the options given below :
Rakesh said, “Shall I play the movie?”
  1. Rakesh said if he could play the movie ?
  2. Rakesh asked that he should play the movie.
  3. Rakesh said if he should play the movie.
  4. Rakesh asked if he should play the movie.
Concept to recallYes/no question → asked if/whether + statement order; shall (asking advice) → should.
  1. Reporting verb for a question: asked; linker if.
  2. ‘Shall I’ becomes ‘he should’, statement order, full stop.
  3. (1), (3) use said; (2) uses that, the linker for statements.

Answer: option (4) — Rakesh asked if he should play the movie.

Q881CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q28NTA final key
Change the sentence given below into an Exclamatory sentence.
Man is a wonderful piece of work.
  1. What piece of work is man !
  2. A piece of work is man !
  3. Man is a wonderful work !
  4. A piece of work, oh! a man.
Concept to recall‘a + adjective + noun’ → ‘What a … + noun + subject + verb!’
  1. The exclamatory form opens with What: ‘What a piece of work is man!’ (Hamlet).
  2. Option (1) is that form; (2) and (3) are not exclamatory structures, (4) is not a sentence.

Answer: option (1) — What piece of work is man !

Q882CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q29NTA final key
Change the sentence into Assertive sentence :
How beautiful is the night !
  1. The beautiful night is today.
  2. The night must be beautiful.
  3. The night is not beautiful.
  4. The night is very beautiful.
Concept to recall‘How + adjective!’ → ‘very + adjective’ in a statement.
  1. Replace How with very; restore statement order.
  2. ‘The night is very beautiful.’

Answer: option (4) — The night is very beautiful.

Q883CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q34NTA final key
From the given options, choose the correct way to end an informed letter.
  1. your faithfully
  2. yours faithfully
  3. yours truly
  4. yours truthfully
Concept to recallFormal letters close with ‘Yours faithfully’ — yours with an s and no apostrophe.
  1. ‘your faithfully’ drops the s; ‘yours truthfully’ is not a closing.
  2. ‘Yours faithfully’ is the standard formal close (the question means a formal letter); ‘yours truly’ is less formal.

Answer: option (2) — yours faithfully

Q884CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q35NTA final key
Arrange the following parts in Letter Writing in its correct sequence :
(A) Date
(B) Subject
(C) Salutation
(D) Sender’s Address
(E) Receiver’s Address
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (A), (B), (E), (D), (C)
  2. (B), (D), (E), (A), (C)
  3. (D), (A), (E), (B), (C)
  4. (C), (D), (E), (A), (B)
Concept to recallFormal letter format (CBSE): sender’s address → date → receiver’s address → subject → salutation → body.
  1. D-A-E-B-C. Note that the salutation comes after the subject line in the school format NTA follows.

Answer: option (3) — (D), (A), (E), (B), (C)

Q885CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q44NTA final key
Use an adverb of manner in the following interrogative sentence :
_________ did you continue it ?
  1. Where
  2. How
  3. When
  4. Why
Concept to recallInterrogative adverbs: how (manner), where (place), when (time), why (reason).
  1. Manner → How.

Answer: option (2) — How

Q886CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q45NTA final key
Identify the type of adverb used in the following sentence :
I am much aliened to have it.
  1. Adverb of Frequency
  2. Adverb of Manner
  3. Adverb of Reason
  4. Adverb of Degree
Concept to recallAdverbs of degree tell how much: much, very, too, quite, almost.
  1. ‘much’ modifies the adjective and tells to what extent → degree.

Answer: option (4) — Adverb of Degree

Q887CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q46NTA final key
Use the correct Question for the given sentence :
I am always on time, _________ ?
  1. amn’t I
  2. am I
  3. aren’t I
  4. wasn’t I
Concept to recallThe negative tag for I am is the irregular aren’t I?
  1. Positive statement → negative tag.
  2. ‘amn’t’ is not standard English, so we use ‘aren’t I?’

Answer: option (3) — aren’t I

Q888CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q50NTA final key
Identify the Adjective Clause in the following sentence :
As the years went by, her prose became more interesting and soon, she was offered a book deal.
  1. As the years went by
  2. her prose became more interesting
  3. and soon, she was offered
  4. a book deal
Concept to recallAn adjective clause qualifies a noun and usually begins with a relative word (who, which, that); a clause beginning with ‘As’ (time) is adverbial.
  1. ‘As the years went by’ is an adverb clause of time; (3) and (4) are fragments.
  2. NTA keys (2): the clause whose complement is the adjective phrase ‘more interesting’.

Answer: option (2) — her prose became more interesting

NoteStrictly the sentence has no adjective (relative) clause: (2) is a main clause with a predicative adjective. NTA’s final key nevertheless gives (2); it is kept as the answer.
Q889CUET 2023 · 2 Jul, Shift 3 · Q16NTA final key
Choose the most appropriate option to convert the following sentence in Active Voice into Passive Voice:
The labourers were digging a canal.
  1. A canal is being dug by the labourers.
  2. A canal was being dug by the labourers.
  3. A canal was dug by the labourers.
  4. A canal had been dug by the labourers.
Concept to recallPast continuous active (were digging) → past continuous passive (was being dug).
  1. Keep the tense: was + being + V3.
  2. (1) present, (3) simple past, (4) past perfect.

Answer: option (2) — A canal was being dug by the labourers.

Q890CUET 2023 · 2 Jul, Shift 3 · Q17NTA final key
Choose the most appropriate option to convert the following sentence in Passive Voice to Active Voice:
Did anyone invite Rachna to the party?
  1. Is Rachna invited to the party?
  2. Had Rachana been invited to the party by anyone?
  3. Was Rachana invited to the party?
  4. Was Rachna going to be invited to the party?
Concept to recallSimple past question with did → passive Was + object + V3?; an indefinite agent (anyone) is dropped.
  1. The given sentence is actually active; its passive is ‘Was Rachna invited to the party?’
  2. ‘by anyone’ is omitted; (2) changes the tense to past perfect, (1) to present.

Answer: option (3) — Was Rachana invited to the party?

NoteThe stem has the direction reversed (it is an active sentence to be made passive).
Q891CUET 2023 · 2 Jul, Shift 3 · Q18NTA final key
Identity the correct conversion of the following sentence in Direct Speech into Indirect Speech:
She said to me, ‘What are you doing?’
  1. She said to me what I was doing.
  2. She asked me what was I to do.
  3. She asked me what I was doing.
  4. She told me what I was doing.
Concept to recallWh-question: said to → asked; statement order; present continuous → past continuous.
  1. ‘She asked me what I was doing.’
  2. (2) keeps question order and changes the meaning; (1), (4) keep said/told.

Answer: option (3) — She asked me what I was doing.

Q892CUET 2023 · 2 Jul, Shift 3 · Q19NTA final key
Identify the correct conversion of the following sentence in Indirect Speech into Direct Speech:
He requested him to wait there till he returned.
  1. He requested to him, ‘Please wait there till I return.’
  2. He said to him ‘Please wait here till I return.’
  3. He requested him, ‘Please wait till I return.’
  4. He said to him, ‘Please wait there till I return.’
Concept to recallIndirect → direct: requested → said to …, ‘Please …’; there → here; returned → return.
  1. The reporting verb becomes said to with Please in the quote.
  2. Place word shifts back: there → here. So (2).
  3. (4) keeps there; (1), (3) keep requested as the reporting verb, and (3) drops the place.

Answer: option (2) — He said to him ‘Please wait here till I return.’

Q893CUET 2023 · 2 Jul, Shift 3 · Q28NTA final key
Change the following sentence from Assertive to Exclamatory:
The chocolates are very bitter.
  1. Such bitterness is in these chocolates!
  2. How bitter these chocolates are!
  3. What bitter are these chocolates!
  4. Very bitter are these chocolates!
Concept to recallvery + adjective → How + adjective + subject + verb!
  1. ‘How bitter these chocolates are!’
  2. What needs a noun (What bitter chocolates!), so (3) is wrong.

Answer: option (2) — How bitter these chocolates are!

Q894CUET 2023 · 2 Jul, Shift 3 · Q29NTA final key
Change the following sentence from Assertive to Exclamatory:
It has been a difficult year.
  1. What difficulty has this year been!
  2. A difficult year indeed has it been!
  3. How difficult of a year it has been!
  4. What a difficult year it has been!
Concept to recalla + adjective + noun → What a + adjective + noun + subject + verb!
  1. ‘What a difficult year it has been!’
  2. (3) ‘How difficult of a year’ is non-standard.

Answer: option (4) — What a difficult year it has been!

Q895CUET 2023 · 2 Jul, Shift 3 · Q34NTA final key
Which of the following is not included in a formal letter?
  1. Subject
  2. Salutation
  3. With lots of love
  4. Date
Concept to recallFormal letters use a formal close (Yours faithfully); affectionate closes belong to informal letters.
  1. Subject, salutation and date are all parts of a formal letter.
  2. ‘With lots of love’ is informal.

Answer: option (3) — With lots of love

Q896CUET 2023 · 2 Jul, Shift 3 · Q35NTA final key
Which of the following is not an appropriate subscription for a formal letter?
  1. yours sincerely
  2. yours lovingly
  3. yours faithfully
  4. yours truly
Concept to recallFormal subscriptions: yours faithfully / sincerely / truly. ‘Yours lovingly’ is for family.
  1. Only ‘yours lovingly’ is informal.

Answer: option (2) — yours lovingly

Q897CUET 2023 · 2 Jul, Shift 3 · Q44NTA final key
Identify the Adverbs used in the given sentences in List I and match them with the type given in List II:
LIST ILIST II
A. Gautam Buddha left his family stealthily.I. adverb of degree
B. I have pleaded enough and now I give up.II. interrogative adverbs
C. How did you come here?III. adverb of manner
D. He has not left the place.IV. adverb of affirmation/negation

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV
  2. A-II, B-III, C-I, D-IV
  3. A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV
  4. A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV
Concept to recallstealthily = manner (how?); enough = degree (how much?); How (in a question) = interrogative adverb; not = negation.
  1. A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV — option (4).
  2. Note that How asks about manner but is classed as an interrogative adverb.

Answer: option (4) — A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV

Q898CUET 2023 · 2 Jul, Shift 3 · Q46NTA final key
Fill in the blank with an appropriate Question Tag:
You think this is funny, ______?
  1. can you
  2. must you
  3. are you
  4. do you
Concept to recallThe tag repeats the auxiliary of the main verb (think → do). A neutral tag would be negative (don’t you?); a same-polarity tag (do you?) expresses surprise or sarcasm.
  1. Main verb ‘think’ (simple present) takes the auxiliary do.
  2. ‘don’t you’ is not offered; ‘do you?’ is the sarcastic same-polarity tag and the only one with the right auxiliary.

Answer: option (4) — do you

Q899CUET 2023 · 2 Jul, Shift 3 · Q50NTA final key
Out of the options given below, choose the sentence which contains an Adjective Clause:
  1. He ate when he was hungry.
  2. I know a place where they sell good food.
  3. He will do it when the time is right.
  4. I am glad that you had a good time.
Concept to recallAn adjective clause qualifies a noun; where can introduce one after a noun of place (a place where …).
  1. ‘where they sell good food’ describes the noun place → adjective clause.
  2. (1), (3) have adverb clauses of time; (4) ‘that you had a good time’ is a noun/adjective-complement clause.

Answer: option (2) — I know a place where they sell good food.

Trapwhere and when do not always begin adverb clauses: after a noun they are relative.

Figures of Speech and Literary Devices15 questions

Q900CUET 2026 · 11 May, Shift 1 · Q35NTA final key
Match the Figures of speech given in List-I with their examples in List-II
List IList II
(A) Hyperbole(I) Dearth dwells in every nook and cranny of the slums.
(B) Simile(II) The fair, funny, fragile looking waif
(C) Personification(III) Malicious words are like bullets that tear through you.
(D) Alliteration(IV) The husband's cruel desertion broke her heart into smithereens.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. A - II, B - I, C - III, D - IV
  2. A - III, B - I, C - IV, D - II
  3. A - IV, B - III, C - I, D - II
  4. A - II, B - IV, C - I, D - III
Concept to recallHyperbole = exaggeration; simile = comparison with like/as; personification = human action given to an abstraction; alliteration = repeated initial sound.
  1. Heart broken “into smithereens” – exaggeration ⇒ A-IV.
  2. Words “like bullets” ⇒ simile, B-III.
  3. Dearth “dwells” (lives) ⇒ personification, C-I.
  4. fair, funny, fragile ⇒ alliteration, D-II.

Answer: option (3) — A - IV, B - III, C - I, D - II

Q901CUET 2026 · 11 May, Shift 1 · Q36NTA final key
Match the expressions given in List I with the appropriate figures of speech given in List II :
List IList II
(A) Her voice crowds up and down the lawn(I) Alliteration
(B) He makes no friend, who never made a foe.(II) Personification
(C) Singing in summer in full-throated ease(III) Hyperbole
(D) Winter laid its icy hands over the city.(IV) Epigram

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. A - II, B - III, C - I, D - IV
  2. A - IV, B - I, C - II, D - III
  3. A - III, B - II, C - I, D - IV
  4. A - III, B - IV, C - I, D - II
Concept to recallEpigram = a brief, witty, paradoxical saying; personification gives hands to winter; “singing in summer” repeats s.
  1. B (no friend without a foe) is a paradoxical saying ⇒ epigram (IV).
  2. D: winter has “icy hands” ⇒ personification (II).
  3. C: singing … summer ⇒ alliteration (I).
  4. A, a voice that fills a whole lawn, is exaggeration ⇒ hyperbole (III).

Answer: option (4) — A - III, B - IV, C - I, D - II

Q902CUET 2026 · 11 May, Shift 1 · Q42NTA final key
Passage (summarised): Dibrugarh and Sambalpur (Q41–45)

Summary in our own words; the exam printed the full travel piece.

With the first chill of the season, India’s forests come back to life. In western Odisha, Dibrugarh Wildlife Sanctuary near Sambalpur, about to be declared India’s newest tiger reserve, is drawing attention “not just for its Wildlife” but also for the local people who have helped it flourish. It spreads over forested slopes by the Hirakud reservoir: birdsong at dawn, spotted deer and langurs, eagles overhead, and on Bot Island “thousands of bats hang like dark fruits”. Once an overlooked woodland, it is now a leading story of eco-tourism and “community-led conservation”.

Sambalpur lies at the edge of this wilderness, along the Mahanadi River, which “runs through it all”. Its past runs from the Chauhan dynasty to colonial times; its present hums with trade, textiles and temple bells.

Nearby, Hirakud Dam (built 1950, one of the world’s longest earthen dams) is called an engineering marvel that tames the Mahanadi. In Sambalpur’s lanes the clicking looms are where the famous Sambalpuri ikat is woven, each fabric made with precision and patience. At festivals people wear ikat saris and handwoven kurtas, and the city becomes a living gallery.

Identify the figure of speech used in the line 'Thousands of bats hang like dark fruits'.
  1. Alliteration
  2. Metaphor
  3. Personification
  4. Simile
Concept to recallSimile = explicit comparison using like or as; metaphor = implied comparison without them.
  1. Bats are compared to dark fruits using “like” ⇒ simile.
  2. No repeated initial sound (not alliteration); bats are not given human traits.

Answer: option (4) — Simile

TrapMetaphor would be “the bats are dark fruits”.
Q903CUET 2026 · 6 Jun, Shift 1 · Q1NTA final key
Identify the figure of speech used in the following lines:-
'The house was crouching on its elbows then,'
Choose the appropriate option from the ones given below:-
  1. Personification
  2. Alliteration
  3. Simile
  4. Hyperbole
Concept to recallPersonification gives a human (or animal) action or body part to a lifeless thing.
  1. A house cannot crouch or have elbows – it is given a human posture ⇒ personification.
  2. No “like/as” (not a simile), no repeated initial sound, no exaggeration.

Answer: option (1) — Personification

Q904CUET 2026 · 6 Jun, Shift 1 · Q12NTA final key
Identify the Figure of Speech used in the given sentence :-
She was impressed to see shining silver spoons at the serving counter.
  1. Pun
  2. Alliteration
  3. Oxymoron
  4. Simile
Concept to recallAlliteration = repetition of the same initial consonant sound in nearby words.
  1. see shining silver spoons … serving ⇒ alliteration.
  2. No double meaning (pun), no contradiction (oxymoron), no “like/as” (simile).

Answer: option (2) — Alliteration

Q905CUET 2026 · 6 Jun, Shift 1 · Q49NTA final key
Passage (summarised): Tao Ying on the bus (Q46–50)

Summary in our own words; the exam printed the full extract of a short story.

When Tao Ying rides the bus alone she often does not buy a ticket, reasoning that the bus, its crew and its fuel cost the same with or without her. She is “astute”: if the conductor looks responsible she buys a ticket at once; if he seems careless, she does not pay, treating it as a small punishment for him and a small saving for herself.

She is a cook in a factory canteen and spends all day beside an open fire baking wheat cakes.

Today her son Xiao Ye is with her. Her jacket catches in the closing door and she wriggles free. “Mama, tickets!” says Xiao Ye – children, the narrator notes, are more conscious of rituals than adults; without a ticket the ride does not feel proper to him. A painted finger on the door marks a height of 1.10 m.

The boy’s hair looks “as fluffy as a bundle of straw”, dry and dull. Tao Ying is “very careful with her purse”, but has “never skimped on her child’s diet”; he is healthy and clever, though his hair is a mess.

The poetic device used in the line 'his hair looks as fluffy as a bundle of straw' is:
  1. metaphor
  2. irony
  3. personification
  4. simile
Concept to recallSimile = comparison with as … as or like.
  1. “as fluffy as a bundle of straw” ⇒ simile.
  2. Metaphor would drop “as … as”.

Answer: option (4) — simile

Q906CUET 2023 · 7 Jun, Shift 1 · Q4NTA final key
Passage (summarised): poem “Love and a Question” (Q1–5)

The paper prints the title “Love and a Question” (a poem by Robert Frost), four stanzas of eight lines. Paraphrase, stanza by stanza:

Stanza I. At evening a stranger comes to the door and speaks politely to the bridegroom. He carries a green-white stick and has nothing with him but his care. He “asked with the eyes more than the lips” for shelter for the night, then turned and looked at the dark road ahead, with no lit window anywhere.

Stanza II. The bridegroom steps into the porch and suggests they both look at the sky and wonder what the night will bring. Woodbine leaves litter the yard, the berries are blue; it is autumn, and winter is already in the wind. He says he wishes he knew.

Stanza III. Inside, the bride sits alone in the dusk bending over the open fire, her face rosy in the glow, thinking of her heart’s desire. The bridegroom looks out at the “weary road” but sees only her within, and wishes he could keep her heart safe, locked in gold.

Stanza IV. He would gladly give the stranger bread, a purse, a heartfelt prayer (or a curse for the rich). What troubles him is whether it is right to let anyone spoil the love of two newly-weds by bringing sorrow into the bridal house. The poem ends with him still uncertain — “the bridegroom wished he knew”.

The phrase 'weary road' is an example of:
  1. Simile
  2. Personification
  3. Metaphor
  4. Transferred epithet
Concept to recallTransferred epithet: an adjective that properly describes a person is transferred to a thing connected with him (sleepless night, weary road).
  1. A road cannot be tired; the weariness belongs to the traveller on it, transferred to the road.
  2. There is no like/as (simile) and no comparison (metaphor); the road is not shown acting like a person, so the precise term is transferred epithet.

Answer: option (4) — Transferred epithet

TrapCalling it personification just because a human quality is attached to a thing.
Q907CUET 2023 · 10 Jun, Shift 2 · Q13NTA final key
Passage (summarised): a Keralite at the Poles

The writer, who grew up in warm, lush green Trivandrum full of sights, sounds and people, finds the Poles quiet. Winter brings an “eerie desolation” and near-silence; survival in the frigid, dark, windy land is only for the fittest, and one misstep can mean anything from an icy injury to a numbing death.

Life there is tenuous but humbling, physically, mentally and spiritually; nature shows its dual face — raw, brutal and unforgiving, yet nurturing and awe-inspiring.

As days shorten most life leaves for warmer lands; those who stay are surrounded by glacial beauty and an unearthly stillness. In midwinter the sun seems only a memory, but auroras of many colours shift and snake “like billowing curtains” across the black sky, a promise that light will return.

Even the emptiness deceives: look closely and a flock of penguins waddles out from behind an ice shelf on the Antarctic peninsula.

Identify the literary device in the sentence given below:
“shimmering displays of blue, red, yellow, green, and orange auroras shifting and snaking like billowing curtains across the pitch black sky...”
Choose the correct option:-
  1. metaphor
  2. alliteration
  3. simile
  4. assonance
Concept to recallSimile: an explicit comparison using like or as. A metaphor compares without them.
  1. The auroras move like billowing curtains → simile.

Answer: option (3) — simile

Trap‘shifting … snaking’ has some sound-play (sibilance), but the device the sentence is built on is the ‘like’ comparison.
Q908CUET 2023 · 15 Jun, Shift 3 · Q14NTA final key
Passage (summarised): from the opening of Chris Cleave’s The Other Hand, with a blurb

The narrator, a young Nigerian woman, says that learning the Queen’s English is like scrubbing the “bright red varnish” off your toe nails on the morning after a dance: it is slow, and a stain of red always remains at the growing edges as a reminder of the good time. She learned it slowly but had plenty of time — two years locked in an immigration detention centre in Essex, in the south-east of the UK.

Why take the trouble? Older girls told her that to survive you must look good or talk even better: the plain and silent ones never seem to have their papers in order, and are repatriated — “sent home early”.

A blurb follows: The Other Hand is about a young woman who flees conflict in her village in the oil-rich region of southern Nigeria, enters the UK illegally and is held for a long time in a detention centre near London. Once freed, she searches for the two English people she knows — she met them years earlier, during a life-changing event on a beach in Nigeria; will they help her, and can she survive as an immigrant?

Learning Queen’s English is described using a metaphor which is :
  1. to learn to survive
  2. a stain of red along the greasing edges
  3. scrubbing off the bright red varnish from your toenails
  4. learning comes slowly
Concept to recallFind the comparison: the learning is likened to removing nail varnish (strictly a simile, as it uses ‘like’).
  1. Learning the Queen’s English is said to be like scrubbing red varnish off one’s toe nails.
  2. The stain of red is a detail within that image, not the comparison itself.

Answer: option (3) — scrubbing off the bright red varnish from your toenails

NoteThe paper calls it a metaphor; with ‘like’ it is technically a simile. The option is unambiguous either way.
Q909CUET 2023 · 18 Jun, Shift 3 · Q3NTA final key
Poem extract (paraphrased): “No Man is an Island” (Q1–5)

The extract, printed under the title “No Man is an Island”, is the well-known passage from John Donne’s Devotions upon Emergent Occasions (Meditation XVII, 1624).

Paraphrase. No human being is complete in himself like an island; each is a piece of a larger continent, part of the mainland. If the sea washes away even one small lump of earth (a “clod”), Europe is made smaller — just as it would be if a whole headland, or the estate of a friend or of one’s own, were lost. In the same way, the death of any person diminishes the speaker, because he is bound up with all mankind. So one should never send to ask whose death the funeral bell is ringing for: “It tolls for thee”.

Form. Several successive lines begin with the same words (“As well as if …”, “No man … / Every man …”), and the whole piece is an extended metaphor of land and sea for human connectedness.

What is the name of the poetic device when there is a repetition of words/phrases at the beginning of successive lines?
  1. Metaphor
  2. Simili
  3. Anaphera
  4. Hyperbole
Concept to recallAnaphora = repetition of a word or phrase at the start of successive lines/clauses (“As well as if … / As well as if …”).
  1. The definition in the question is that of anaphora (spelt “Anaphera” in the paper).
  2. Metaphor and simile are comparisons; hyperbole is exaggeration.

Answer: option (3) — Anaphera

Q910CUET 2023 · 21 Jun, Shift 1 · Q5NTA final key
Passage (summarised): a Brahman in search of the Ganges (F. W. Bain)

An old Brahman, carrying his pot and staff, is doing penance “for the expiation of sin” on the banks of what he believes is the Ganges. A passing Pashupata ascetic laughs at him: this miserable puddle has nothing to do with the Ganges, which is hundreds of miles away and dwarfs this brook as Mount Meru dwarfs an ant-hill. Thanking him, the Brahman travels on to a broad river, rejoices, and bathes in it daily for five years — until a Kapalika tells him he is wasting his time on a river of no sanctity: is a jackal a lion, or a Chandala a Brahman? Sighing, the Brahman again takes up pot and staff.

Now old and weakened by penance, he toils on through the heat; the sun beats on his head “like the thunderbolt of Indra” and gives him fever. At last he collapses, drags himself up a low hill, and sees the mighty Ganges below, crowded with pilgrims. Crying out to Mother Ganges that he has pursued her all his life only to die helpless in sight of her, he dies of a broken heart without reaching its shore.

(The file as mirrored begins the passage at the ascetic’s arrival; any earlier opening is not shown.)

The sun heat on the Brahman’s head like _______________.
  1. a shining sword
  2. the thunderbolt of Indira
  3. a heavy hammer
  4. a bright star
Concept to recallSimile: the sun beat on his head ‘like the thunderbolt of Indra’ (printed ‘Indira’ in the option).
  1. The passage compares the sun to Indra’s thunderbolt (vajra).
  2. The other images are not in the text.

Answer: option (2) — the thunderbolt of Indira

  2. Detiriorate
  3. Deteriorate
  4. Detriorate
Concept to recalldeteriorate = de-terior-ate (Latin deterior, “worse”): five syllables, -erior- in the middle.
  1. Say it: de-te-ri-o-rate. Each syllable has its own vowel: d-e-t-e-r-i-o-r-a-t-e.
  2. The others drop or swap a vowel (Di-, -tiri-, Detr-) or the final -e.

Answer: option (3) — Deteriorate
